Partial-rollout checkpointing for NeMo Gym and NeMo RL

Design v2 on the environment-server architecture, with the v1 proposal preserved · draft for review

A long agentic rollout should survive a trainer checkpoint and a crash without being thrown away. This page walks through the lifecycle message by message: a normal episode, a checkpoint taken in place, a crash followed by a restore, a straggler that misses the deadline, and a generation that is cut mid-decode. Each step shows who sends what to whom and what every component's state machine is doing.

Part 1

The problem

Why checkpoint rollouts that are still running

Reinforcement-learning training periodically checkpoints the trainer so it can survive a crash or a preemption. Agentic rollouts make that hard: a multi-turn rollout with tool calls, a software-engineering task, or a long judged conversation can run for minutes or hours, and thousands run at once. There are two simple answers, and both fail at scale:

  • Restart every unfinished rollout after a crash. Every token already generated and every tool call already run is thrown away, and long rollouts may never finish between failures.
  • Wait for every rollout to finish before checkpointing. Checkpoint latency becomes the latency of the slowest rollout, and one hung tool call or harness blocks the checkpoint indefinitely.

Partial-rollout checkpointing takes a consistent snapshot while rollouts are in flight, then continues each one from its last safe point after a crash, without repeating work that has side effects and without waiting for stragglers.

The state a running rollout spreads across

One rollout is not one process. At any moment its state lives in several places:

WhereWhat must survive a crash
Environment server (Gym)Where the episode is in its protocol: which step runs next, which sessions it opened, and the results of steps already done
Agent server (Gym)The turn loop: the conversation so far, tool calls not yet answered, and session cookies
Resources server (Gym)Environment state per session, such as a counter, a database, or a document store that tools change
Policy model server (Gym)The token-free lineage of model calls, and which responses have not been delivered yet
Inference workers (training framework)Generated tokens, including the prefix of a generation still decoding
Training frameworkThe durable token store, the registry of dispatched rollouts, and the global checkpoint itself

Every rollout also has an identity that survives retries and restores: a stable rollout ID plus an attempt number. After a restore the rollout continues as the next attempt, and nothing of an older attempt may still be running anywhere.

What a correct checkpoint requires

  • One consistent cut. Every component's saved state describes the same moment of the same rollout.
  • No repeated side effects. A step that changes state is never run twice because of a restore.
  • Bounded latency. A checkpoint never waits for a generation or a slow rollout to finish; the controller can retire a straggler, which then restarts from its input.
  • Durable before published. Every component's files are complete and verified before the global checkpoint names them.
  • Retired work stops. Retiring an attempt stops its work everywhere before it returns, so nothing from a replaced attempt can still change state.
  • Nothing grows without an end of life. Every piece of state has an owner and an event that frees it; a restart does not count.
  • Fail closed. A server that cannot continue a rollout still takes part, so it can never silently produce a checkpoint that is wrong.

How it fits with NeMo RL

The training framework owns the global checkpoint transaction; Gym owns everything inside Gym.

  1. Prepare. The framework stops dispatching new rollouts, pauses its trainer and trajectory assembler actors until resume, and asks Gym to prepare. Gym brings every in-flight rollout to a safe point, in the order Gym defines, and reports any straggler it had to wait for.
  2. Commit. Gym writes each server's state into the framework's checkpoint directory. The framework saves its own state (token store, rollout registry, dataloader) alongside, and waits for results of rollouts that finished just before the cut.
  3. Publish, then resume. The framework publishes the checkpoint atomically and tells Gym to resume.
  4. Restore after a crash. The framework starts fresh Gym servers, restores Gym's state for the rollouts it will continue, and re-dispatches each of them as its next attempt, which continues from its last safe point.

Part 2 is how v2 does this. Part 3 is the first proposal, kept as it was. Part 4 compares them.

What can go wrong

Saving a running rollout has many race conditions, edge cases and failure cases, and a list of incidents would never be complete. This section derives them instead:

  • It starts from a model of the system and of what can fail in it.
  • It states what a correct checkpoint means in that model.
  • It walks through each class of hazard the model allows. For each class it gives:
    • one concrete example;
    • the invariant the design keeps;
    • the mechanism that keeps it;
    • the section of this page that describes the mechanism in detail.

The goal is that every mechanism in the v2 design can be traced back to a hazard it exists to prevent.

The system and what can fail in it

A Gym deployment is a set of processes that exchange HTTP requests.

  • The controller, such as a trainer or an evaluation run, sends each rollout to an environment server as a /run request.
  • The environment server starts sessions on an agent server and a resources server, invokes the agent, and asks the resources server to verify the result.
  • The agent calls the policy model server, which forwards each generation to its inference workers, and it calls the resources server's tools.
  • Any of these servers can run several uvicorn workers that share one port, so a single server is itself several processes.

Some of the state a rollout depends on lives outside every server process, so it survives a crash of the process that created it:

  • the policy model server's capture ledger files, which record the token-free lineage of each attempt's model calls;
  • sandboxes and remote harnesses that a resources server or an agent started, which can keep running after the server that started them has died;
  • the checkpoint directory, which the controller owns and every server writes its part of a checkpoint into;
  • the controller's own records, such as the evaluation run's dispatch log and the trainer's own checkpoint.

The participants of one rollout. Every solid arrow is a request whose reply can still be on its way when a checkpoint is taken, plain lines connect a server to state it keeps outside its process, and every server can be several worker processes.

The design assumes the following can happen, in any combination:

  • Any process can crash at any instruction. That includes one worker of a server, a whole server, every Gym server at once, and the controller itself.
  • Any call can time out or fail. A call that fans out to several servers can succeed on some of them and fail on others, and a call that timed out on the caller's side may still finish on the server's side.
  • Clients send requests again. Gym's HTTP client resends a request after a dropped connection, a model harness retries a model call after a timeout, and a controller repeats a control call that failed.
  • Messages take time to arrive. A request or a reply can be on the wire while the sender, the receiver or both change state, and two requests sent on different connections can arrive in either order.
  • Disks can fail mid-write. A write can stop halfway through a file, and two writers can write into the same directory.

The design does not assume that servers lie about what they can save, or that anyone other than the controller holds the control bearer token. The assumptions section lists everything else it relies on.

What a correct checkpoint means

A checkpoint holds one saved state per participant, and it is correct when those states together form a consistent cut: a set of states that could all have been observed at one moment of every rollout, even though they were saved at different times. For Gym this comes down to two conditions.

  1. Every effect a saved state depends on is in the checkpoint. If an agent's saved conversation contains a tool result, the resources server's saved state contains the change that tool call made. A saved state may be behind some effect, such as a model call the model server recorded but the agent never received, as long as the second condition covers that effect.
  2. Nothing the checkpoint holds is done again in a way that changes the result. Work that happened after a participant's saved state will run again when the rollout continues after a crash, so that work must either be safe to repeat or be prevented from repeating.

Two more requirements from what the design must guarantee shape the answers: a checkpoint must not wait for long work such as a generation, and every piece of state the mechanism creates must have an event that frees it. Each hazard class below is one way the failure model above can break one of these conditions.

Work in flight at the moment of the cut

What goes wrong. Servers keep working while a checkpoint is taken, and a step that changes state can straddle the moment each server is saved:

  1. An agent's turn loop for rollout r sends a tool call that adds a row to the resources server's database.
  2. The agent's state is saved from before the tool call.
  3. The tool call finishes, and the resources server's state is saved with the new row.
  4. After a crash the restored agent sends the tool call again, and the database now holds the row twice.

The same shape appears with a generation that is half finished, a verification that changes state, and a session start that is still creating a sandbox.

Invariant. Every participant saves a rollout at the same boundary, which is a point between steps. A step that changes state is either entirely before that boundary in every participant's saved state or entirely after it.

Mechanism. Each episode records a boundary after every step, and every step in flight has one of two step types.

  • A wait step is one the checkpoint waits for. The episode then stops at the next boundary with the step's result.
  • A replay step is one the checkpoint does not wait for:
    • the episode counts as stopped at the boundary before it, and the step runs again after a crash;
    • a result it produces while the checkpoint is open waits at the next boundary until resume.
  • A replay step that raises while the checkpoint is open stops at a cleared boundary instead and waits there until resume.
    • It does not hold up the checkpoint, which saves the episode with no boundary so that it starts over from its input after a crash.
    • Its cleanup and its /run reply both wait for resume, so the episode cannot end while Gym is prepared.
  • In single_agent_turn every stage starts with its boundary, including the agent close and the final return. This matters for a restored rollout:
    • After a restore and resume, a later checkpoint can prepare before the replacement /run arrives, and the replacement is then admitted while admission is closed.
    • Because its stage starts with the boundary it was restored from, it parks there before doing any work: it closes no session, does not finish, stays ready, and the commit saves the same boundary.
    • A boundary recorded after the stage's first action would let a replacement close the agent, or run final cleanup and end, while Gym is prepared.
  • When an agent activation fails, the environment server closes the agent session at once to keep the agent's observations. During a checkpoint that close comes after the failed step has parked, so it too waits for resume.
  • Inside an agent, the tool calls of one round run between two boundaries, so the agent's prepare waits for the round to finish.
  • Resources servers are prepared last, so the tool calls they are serving are still admitted and finish first.
  • Generations are the exception that keeps checkpoints fast: the checkpoint does not wait for them, holds their responses instead, and can save their prefix as an optional cut.

Described in. How episodes are saved, how agents are saved, how the policy model avoids waiting and the order Gym checkpoints servers in.

Messages that cross the cut

What goes wrong. A request sent before a checkpoint can have its reply arrive after it. Then the sender's saved state and the receiver's saved state disagree about whether the exchange happened:

  1. The environment server invokes the agent for rollout r. This is a replay step, so the environment server's checkpoint counts the episode at the boundary before the invocation.
  2. The agent's turn loop finishes and the agent sends its reply, which is still on the wire when the checkpoint is taken.
  3. The agent's saved session shows the turn loop as finished, while the environment server's saved episode still has the invocation ahead of it.
  4. After a crash the restored environment server invokes the agent again. Without care, the agent would run a second turn loop, with new model and tool calls, on a session that already ran one.

Every arrow in the system figure has the same shape. A model response can be on its way to the agent, a session start can be on its way to the agent or the resources server, and a /run reply can be on its way to the controller.

Invariant. Each exchange that crosses the cut is handled the same way on both sides. Either the receiver's saved state includes the reply, or the sender's effect is left out of the checkpoint, or repeating the request produces the same reply.

Where a reply can be when the cut is taken, and how each kind of exchange is resolved.

Mechanism. Each kind of exchange has its own rule:

  • Agent to policy model. When the model closes admission it holds every response that has not started, and the checkpoint leaves those calls' ledger rows out. A response the model finished sending just before it prepared can still reach the agent while the checkpoint is open. The agent then holds that reply and stays at the boundary before the call until resume. If Gym crashes before resume, the restored agent makes the call again, and the token-capture builder treats the two calls with the same prompt as a client retry and keeps the one the agent continued from.
  • Environment server to agent. Runs are idempotent.
    • The environment server sends the run's index in the x-ng-agent-activation header, and the agent saves the reply of its last finished run with the session.
    • A repeated run with that index gets the saved reply without running anything.
    • An index that is neither the last finished run nor the next one is refused with checkpoint_activation_out_of_order.
    • A request for a run that is still going waits for it to end and then gets its reply, so a retried request is never refused while the first one finishes.
    • Before it replays or starts a run, the agent checks the attempt the request's rollout path names against the session's, so the harness of a crashed attempt cannot drive or read a restored session.
    • A legacy /run sends index 1 on the call to its own turn loop. A checkpoint taken after the loop replied, but before /run moved on, therefore restores the reply instead of running the loop again.
  • Agent session close.
    • A session close waits for the checkpoint to end while the agent's admission is closed. It checks admission before it marks the session as closing, so a commit always finds the session open and saves it.
    • This cannot stall prepare through an episode's final cleanup, which closes the agent session:
      • coordination prepares environment servers before agents;
      • an episode in final cleanup keeps its environment server from being ready, so its close reaches the agent before the agent closes admission.
    • A close stops the session's run before it runs the agent's own cleanup, so the run never acts on state that is already released.
    • On every agent, a call to an agent's /v1/responses outside any session is reported as a restart while it runs, and one without a rollout path is refused.
    • Simple Agent saves each turn without its question, which repeats the request's input and earlier outputs, and rebuilds it on restore, so the saved state grows with the turns rather than with their square.
  • Environment server to agent and resources server, for session starts. The environment server chooses each session ID before it starts the session and saves it in the boundary, and a session start is safe to repeat for the same ID and episode. A session start already in progress when admission closes holds up prepare on the agent and resources server until its session is registered, and one that arrives later waits for resume. A restored session that its next attempt starts again is reused rather than created twice.
  • Environment server to resources server, for verification. A verification declared safe to repeat is admitted during a checkpoint and not waited for. The session it ends stays in the checkpoint until resume, because the episode's boundary is still before the verification.
  • Environment server to controller.
    • An episode that finishes during prepare stops at its final boundary with its result instead of replying.
    • An episode whose replay step failed while the checkpoint is open also replies only after resume, so its rollout is still in flight for the controller, which names it in the commit.
    • A reply that was already on the wire is the controller's to collect: before it builds its own list, it waits for every outstanding /run whose rollout is neither in the commit nor a restart.
    • It never waits for a restart. A restart is never in the commit's scope, so it keeps running through the checkpoint, and after a crash it starts over from its input.

Described in. How the policy model avoids waiting, how agents are saved, how resources servers declare their state, situations a real run hits and what any controller must do.

Effects repeated on replay

What goes wrong. In this failure model, work runs at least once rather than exactly once. A restore repeats everything after a participant's saved state, and clients resend requests on their own:

  1. The resources server for rollout r runs /verify, which writes the reward to an external store and frees the session's sandbox.
  2. Gym crashes before the environment server records the boundary after verification.
  3. After a restore the episode continues at the boundary before verification and calls /verify again, which writes the reward a second time or fails because the sandbox is gone.

A repeated session start can create a second sandbox, a repeated model call adds a second generation to the ledger, and a repeated /run runs the whole attempt twice.

Invariant. A step that will run again after a restore is one that has been declared safe to repeat. Every other step is waited for, and its result is recorded so it never runs a second time.

Mechanism. Only steps that are safe to repeat are replay steps.

  • Session starts are safe because the session ID is chosen by the caller and saved before the start.
  • Agent runs are safe because the agent answers a repeated run with its saved reply.
  • Verification is a wait step unless the resources server declares checkpoint_verify = "replay", which it reports on every session start's reply in x-ng-checkpoint-verify.
    • The verification's result is recorded at the episode's last boundary, so a restore never verifies twice.
  • A repeated model call is resolved by the capture builder's retry groups:
    • When a client retried a call the model was still running, only the cut of the latest call is kept.
    • After each cut round, the newest cut of a call also replaces the restored cut that a live retry of that call would continue. The new checkpoint keeps only the newest cut's staged rows, so a retry never receives a cut whose staged rows may already be deleted.
    • With several workers, a retry of a call that already used its restored cut is generated again instead.
  • With checkpointing on, Gym's client never sends a /run again after a dropped connection: the controller retires the attempt instead and sends the next one.

Described in. How episodes are saved, how resources servers declare their state, how agents are saved and choices and the alternatives they rule out.

Stale actors

What goes wrong. Something that the rest of the system has given up on can keep running and keep sending requests:

  1. The controller retires attempt 0 of rollout r and sends attempt 1.
  2. Just before its own retire, the agent sent a model call for attempt 0 on a different connection than the retire.
  3. That call reaches the policy model after the model has finished retiring attempt 0. Without a fence it is accepted, and its rows land in the capture files next to attempt 1's.

The same thing happens with a harness in a remote sandbox that outlives a crash, a client that retries a request of a retired attempt, and a delayed control call from a controller that has already moved on, such as a prepare for a checkpoint that was already resumed.

Invariant. Once an attempt is retired, or replaced by a restore, no server accepts work from it or from an earlier attempt of the same rollout until the controller declares the rollout finished.

  • The one deliberate exception is a session close: a resources server still accepts /close_session from a retired attempt, because that close is how the server frees the session's state.
  • A close or a verification must come from the attempt that owns the session, so after a restore the replaced attempt cannot end its replacement's session.
  • A request on a session a restore installed must name its attempt, by its rollout prefix or its MCP token, since the replaced attempt holds the same session cookie.
  • With checkpointing on, every activation of an agent session must name its attempt in its rollout path as well, restored or not.
    • After a restore the session's own record already names the replacement, so it cannot stand in for a missing path.
    • An activation without one is refused with checkpoint_rollout_id_required.
  • Once a checkpoint ID has been resumed, no call can reopen it.

How each server treats a request from something that is no longer current.

Mechanism. Every request of a rollout carries its rollout ID and attempt number in the /ng-rollout/<id> path prefix.

  • The suffix -a<N> is reserved for the attempt: an explicit rollout ID <id>-a<N> always means attempt N of <id>, which is how NeMo RL names a restored attempt. No rollout's own ID can be mistaken for another rollout's attempt.
  • A retire raises the rollout's retire mark on every server before it stops anything, never lowers it, and keeps it even if the retire fails, so a late request is refused with 409 checkpoint_stale_attempt.
    • The mark is raised before any work the retire's deadline limits, so even a retire that arrives too late to stop anything still leaves it.
    • On a server with several workers the mark reaches every worker, and a worker that joins later receives the current marks.
    • The mark is a single entry per rollout and is dropped only by an explicit forget.
  • On the policy model, retiring an attempt also retires its capture ledger, which leaves a fence on disk so a late call's tokens are never captured.
  • A policy call that is still waiting at closed admission when its attempt is marked retired is refused for good:
    • it stays refused after forget, and even if the retire was cut short;
    • the retire returns only after every such waiting call has left.
  • Checkpoint IDs are fenced too:
    • Only one checkpoint can be active at a time, and a call naming another is refused with checkpoint_conflict.
    • Resume remembers the checkpoint ID, so a delayed call for it is refused with checkpoint_stale. Gym keeps the last 64 resumed IDs for this.

Retire marks live in memory, so a crash loses them.

  • For a rollout that continues from the checkpoint, the restore puts the refusal back: before any work its deadline limits, every participant, and every worker of each participant, marks every episode in the restore's scope as retired up to the attempt the restore replaces.
    • A harness of that attempt that outlived the crash, for example in a remote sandbox, is therefore refused with checkpoint_stale_attempt by the restored servers.
    • These marks also end only through forget.
  • A rollout that starts over is in no restore's scope, so the controller must retire its last recorded attempt before it sends the next one.
  • The agent's restore hook must still stop whatever the crashed process left running, because a harness can act on its sandbox without calling Gym.

Described in. How Gym abandons an attempt, the state machine every server runs and rollouts that cannot be saved.

Partial failure of calls that span servers

What goes wrong. Every control call reaches several servers separately, so it can finish on some and fail on others:

  1. The controller retires attempt 0 of rollout r. The environment and agent stages succeed.
  2. The last stage reaches the policy model and the resources server together. The resources server succeeds, but the policy model times out while it waits for a cancelled generation to stop.
  3. Coordination reports the retire as failed, and the controller cannot tell what state each server is in.

A commit can likewise write some servers' manifests and not others, a restore can install state on some servers, and a forget can drop its entry on some servers and not on others.

Invariant. A call that finished only partly never leaves a state the controller would act on, and repeating the same call with the same arguments converges on the state a single successful call would have produced.

What happens when a control call fails on some servers. Restore undoes itself, and every other call converges when the controller repeats it.

Mechanism. Every call can be repeated with the same checkpoint ID.

  • Each server remembers the result of every call it finished, together with the arguments it ran with, and returns the same result to a repeat.
    • A repeat with different arguments, such as another directory or another list of rollouts, is refused with checkpoint_conflict.
    • A retire that already finished finds nothing left to stop.
  • Restore is all-or-nothing: if any server fails, coordination retires the new attempts everywhere, which frees what was installed, then resumes every server and raises the error.
    • A server that cannot reopen admission after its restore failed stays closed. The next resume, under any checkpoint ID, tries the reopen again instead of answering that there is nothing left to resume.
  • Forget is checked on every worker of a server before any worker drops its entry. A resources server refuses it with checkpoint_retire_incomplete if its retire has not yet freed every session of the rollout, or if it still has a session start of a retired attempt in flight.
  • A commit checks again that the server is still ready.
    • It fails with 409 checkpoint_export_failed if something moved since prepare before the server's export started, or if the export fails, which includes a server with several workers losing one between the readiness check and the snapshot.
    • Every later commit for that checkpoint ID gets the same error, because a second export could take a later cut than the other servers committed. The controller then resumes and prepares again under a new checkpoint ID.
    • Storing records that were already exported is still repeated.
  • A checkpoint is not valid until the controller publishes it, and the controller does that only after every commit succeeded.
  • If the controller disappears, each server's lease expires and it resumes on its own, trying again after any error until it has reopened.
  • The rest is the controller's job: it repeats every call that failed until it succeeds.

Described in. The order Gym checkpoints servers in, the state machine every server runs and what any controller must do.

Operations that outlive their deadline

What goes wrong. A deadline ends the call that waits for some work, but not always the work itself:

  1. A commit starts writing a server's records in a thread, and the call's deadline passes while the thread is still writing.
  2. The call returns checkpoint_deadline_exceeded, and the controller retries the commit.
  3. A naive retry would export the server's state again, taking a later cut than the other servers already committed, while the first thread could still publish its own manifest later, even after the controller has resumed.

The same holds for the cleanup that deletes restored state a commit leaves out, for a restore's install, and for exporting the state of many sessions.

Invariant. Work started for a call either finishes as the same work that every repeat of the call waits for, or it is stopped before it can publish anything. After resume returns, nothing a deadline abandoned can still change what the checkpoint holds.

Mechanism. The export, the write and the cleanup each run as a task that the caller's deadline cannot cancel, and a repeated commit waits for the same task, so a checkpoint's state is taken exactly once.

  • If storing failed, the repeat stores the same records again.
  • If the export itself failed, the checkpoint is over: every repeat is refused with checkpoint_export_failed, because exporting again could take a later cut than the other servers committed.
  • Resume stops a write that is still running. The writer checks a stop flag before every record, and its last check, the rename of its records file and the creation of the manifest all happen under a lock that resume also takes, so no manifest can appear once resume has returned.
  • Resume cancels an export nobody will use.
  • Resume waits for restored state that is still being deleted, because a new attempt may start as the attempt being deleted. If its deadline passes first it reports the deadline and stays closed for a repeat.
  • A restore whose install outlives its deadline reopens admission only once the install has finished.
    • A resume that arrives first waits for that install within its own deadline and then reopens.
    • A retire waits for the install before freeing what it brings.
  • Retire and restore both raise their marks before any work their deadline limits, so a call that arrives after its deadline still leaves the refusal in place.
  • The generation cut request gets only half of the time left for prepare, so a stuck inference worker cannot use up the later stages' time.

Described in. How a checkpoint is written, how a checkpoint is restored and how the policy model avoids waiting.

Concurrency inside one server

What goes wrong. Inside one server process, control calls and data requests run concurrently on one event loop, and several of them can act on the same session at once:

  1. The controller retires attempt 0 of rollout r. The agent cancels the session's running turn loop and waits for it to stop.
  2. The retire's deadline passes before the turn loop has stopped.
  3. Meanwhile the environment server's cleanup closes the same agent session. If the close cancelled the turn loop a second time, it would interrupt the cleanup that the first cancellation started.

Other examples are the same session being started twice at once by a client retry, a restore arriving while a session start is in progress, and an activation that starts just as prepare closes admission.

Invariant. Each operation on a session or an episode takes effect once, and an operation that is cut short leaves its target tracked, so a repeat finds it and waits for it again.

Mechanism. Session starts are counted per session and attempt, and a retire waits for every start of its attempts so it can free what they build.

  • A session start that still finishes after its attempt was retired, for example because the retire was cut short while it waited, leaves a retired session:
    • its requests are refused and it is never exported;
    • it holds up every checkpoint until a repeated retire frees it;
    • forget is refused while such a start is in flight or such a session is not yet freed.
  • Marking an attempt retired refuses its existing sessions at once, before the retire waits for anything, so a retire cut short or arriving after its deadline still leaves them refused. Forget is refused while any tracked session of the rollout belongs to an attempt at or below the mark.
  • A retire does not wait for a protocol route, such as a Gymnasium /reset, that was admitted before the retire but starts its session after the retire returned.
    • That session also lands as a retired session, and forget returns checkpoint_retire_incomplete until a repeated retire frees it.
    • This is safe but costs the controller another retire round.
  • A retire, and a commit's deletion of restored state its scope leaves out, stop many episodes at once up to a fixed bound, but each rollout only once, through the latest attempt named, so no two stops of one rollout overlap.
  • Retire and close each cancel a running task at most once, and a session stays tracked, holding up the next checkpoint, until its turn loop has stopped.
  • Once an episode's final cleanup has started, a retire waits for it instead of cancelling it.
  • A resources server records a session start or end as soon as its response starts, before the reply is sent. A client that disconnects while the reply is on its way cancels the request, and recording the change any later would lose it.
  • Restore refuses a process that already has live episodes, live sessions, session starts or requests in progress, or served model calls.
  • An activation that starts while prepare is closing admission stops at its first boundary.
  • An episode becomes a restart only once no checkpoint is open, so the list of restarts never changes during a checkpoint.
  • Phase changes in the control plane are serialized by one lock, while prepare waits for readiness outside it, so a resume can interrupt a prepare that is waiting.

Described in. How agents are saved, how Gym abandons an attempt, rollouts that cannot be saved and situations a real run hits.

State with no end of life

What goes wrong. Every mechanism above keeps something: a retire mark, a restored session, a ledger fence. In a run of millions of rollouts, anything without an explicit end of life grows until a restart:

  1. The controller restores 1,000 rollouts from a checkpoint, then decides to send only 800 of them again.
  2. Every server still holds the restored state of the other 200, and nothing will ever claim it.
  3. Each later checkpoint saves that state again, and the servers keep it for the rest of the run.

Invariant. Every piece of state the mechanism creates has an owner and an explicit event that frees it. Neither a restart nor a time limit counts as such an event.

Mechanism. Retire frees an attempt's state before it replies, and forget drops the retire mark once the controller knows the rollout can never run again.

  • A restore leaves the same mark for each attempt it replaces, so the controller forgets restored rollouts as well as retired ones.
  • A resources server's retire calls its retire_session_state hook in every mode, so a restart_only or stateless server that keeps per-session state frees it there.
  • A resources session that is registered after its attempt was retired is freed by a repeated retire. Forget returns checkpoint_retire_incomplete until then, so the controller cannot drop the refusal while the session still exists.
  • Restored state that a commit's list leaves out is deleted by that commit, without a mark or a ledger fence, so the controller can still start the rollout over as that attempt.
    • On policy model servers that share one capture ledger, that deletion skips every attempt one of them has marked as started, so one server never deletes the rows another is continuing.
    • The ledger is deleted before the server drops its own record of the restored attempt, so a deletion that fails is tried again by the repeated commit.
  • Capture ledgers are retired and deleted by the controller through the routes from #3938 and #3939.
  • Each server remembers at most 64 resumed checkpoint IDs, and the results it remembers for a checkpoint are dropped when that checkpoint is resumed.
  • The evaluation controller:
    • repeats failed retires before the next checkpoint and when the run ends;
    • forgets each rollout it retired or restored once an attempt sent after that replies, and forgets the rest when the run ends.

Described in. How Gym abandons an attempt, how a checkpoint is restored, choices and the alternatives they rule out and evaluation runs as the controller.

Placement across workers

What goes wrong. A server with several uvicorn workers serves each connection on whichever worker accepts it, while each session's state lives only in the worker that created it:

  1. A resources server runs four workers, and worker 2 creates the session of rollout r.
  2. A tool call for that session is accepted by worker 3, which has no state for it and would run it against an empty session.
  3. A checkpoint call accepted by worker 1 would see only worker 1's sessions, and after a restore into two workers, the cookie of rollout r still names worker 2, which no longer exists.

Invariant. A server with several workers acts as one participant, each session's requests reach the one worker that holds the session, and a checkpoint holds exactly one record per session.

Mechanism. A coordinator in the server's main process owns the participant and tells every worker when to close, reopen, retire, export and install.

  • Prepare is ready only once every configured worker has reported ready.
  • A worker lost while a checkpoint is open holds up the checkpoint until resume, because what it held is unknown.
  • A worker lost after the commit checked readiness but before the snapshot took its records with it. That commit fails with 409 checkpoint_export_failed, and the controller prepares again under a new checkpoint ID.
  • Each session's requests reach the worker that holds it through a routing claim: one file per session ID, in a directory the workers share, naming that worker.
    • The router reads the session ID the client already sends, from the session cookie, the MCP session token, or the body of a session start or close.
    • A request is forwarded to that worker's private socket, or refused with 410 if that worker is gone.
  • Restore installs each restored session on a live worker and rewrites its routing claim to name that worker.
  • Episode state that lives inside one request stays with the coordinator until exactly one worker claims it.
  • A commit that finds the same session on two workers keeps the live copy and frees the stale one.
  • A policy model server refuses to restore once any of its workers has left, because the replacement cannot report what the old worker served.

Described in. Servers with several workers and known gaps.

Components that cannot be saved

What goes wrong. Some components have no way to save their state, such as an agent whose harness is opaque and has no session hooks, or a resources server whose state is a live process it cannot snapshot:

  1. Rollout q uses such a resources server, and rollout r does not.
  2. If the checkpoint saved q's agent and environment state but not its resources state, a restored q would continue against a fresh environment its conversation never saw.
  3. If the checkpoint instead waited for q to finish, one such rollout would hold up the checkpoint of r and of every other rollout in the run.

Invariant. A rollout is continued only if every server it touched can save its part. A rollout that cannot be saved is never saved in part and never holds up any other rollout.

Mechanism. Every server takes part in every checkpoint, and a server that cannot save its state takes part as restart-only:

  • agents without hooks;
  • resources servers in restart_only mode, which is the default;
  • environment protocols that record no boundaries.
  • Such a server says so on the reply to a session start with x-ng-checkpoint-restart, and the environment server marks the episode as a restart once no checkpoint is open.
  • A restart_only server also lists the episode of every session start still in flight as a restart, because that start's reply will say so and prepare does not wait for it.
  • Prepare lists the restarts but never waits for them.
    • The controller leaves them out of the commit with PrepareResult.continued.
    • A commit that names one anyway is refused with checkpoint_restart_in_scope.
  • Every participant exports only live records inside the commit's scope, so nothing retired is ever written, and neither is any part of a rollout that another participant reports as a restart.
  • A restart keeps running through the checkpoint. After a crash the controller retires its old attempt everywhere and sends it again from its input.

Described in. Rollouts that cannot be saved and how resources servers declare their state.

Storage failures

What goes wrong. The checkpoint directory is written by many processes, and any of them can fail mid-write:

  1. A server's commit is halfway through its records file when the host loses power.
  2. A repeated commit for the same checkpoint writes into the same directory while the first write's thread is still running.
  3. Later the controller restores from that directory, and without checks it would install a truncated or mixed set of records.

Invariant. A manifest names exactly one complete records file, along with its digest and record count, and a directory that has a manifest never changes. A restore that finds anything else fails with a typed error instead of installing part of a state.

Mechanism. Each server writes its records durably, in this order:

  1. It writes its records to a temporary file, one at a time, hashing them as it goes, then flushes and syncs the file and renames it after its SHA-256 digest.
  2. Before it publishes the manifest, the commit syncs the parent of every directory from the participant's own directory up to the controller's checkpoint directory, so a host crash cannot lose a directory entry under a committed manifest.
  3. The manifest is written last, synced, and created with a hard link, which never replaces an existing name.
  • A repeated commit that finds its manifest already published syncs the participant's directory before it reports success, because the write that published the manifest may have failed before syncing it. A commit that reports success is always durable.
  • Two writers of the same records end with the same file. If two writers race with different records, exactly one manifest is created and the other writer removes its own records file and fails.
  • Restore checks the manifest's schema, server kind and name, the records file's digest and record count, and the shape of every record it installs. Any mismatch fails the restore with HTTP 422 checkpoint_invalid_state.
  • The controller publishes a checkpoint only after every commit succeeded, and deletes the directories it does not keep, including ones from commits it never published.

Described in. How a checkpoint is written and what any controller must do.

Assumptions and dependencies

The guarantees above hold only while the assumptions in this section hold. Each one is stated so that it can be checked, together with what breaks when it does not hold. Where the answer is that Gym fails closed, the result is a refused call, a failed checkpoint or a rollout that starts over, never a rollout that continues from an inconsistent state.

What the controller must do

The full list of rules is in what any controller must do. The table below restates each one with its consequence, and adds three that follow from the code.

The controllerIf it does not
Is the only controller of the deployment, and keeps the control bearer token to itself.Checkpoint calls of two controllers refuse each other with checkpoint_conflict, but /run, retire and forget are not tied to a checkpoint, so one controller could retire or forget the other's rollouts.
Stops sending rollouts and consuming results between prepare and resume.A new /run is refused with 409 checkpoint_admission_closed, and capture ledger retire and delete are refused with 409. A consumer that acts on results in that window can make the controller's own checkpoint disagree with Gym's.
Commits exactly the rollouts it continues: PrepareResult.continued of what is in flight, plus every restored rollout it has not sent again yet.A commit that names a restart fails with checkpoint_restart_in_scope. A restored rollout left out of the list has its restored state deleted by that commit and must start over.
Waits for every outstanding /run whose rollout is neither in the commit nor a restart before it builds its list, and never waits for a restart, which keeps running through the checkpoint and starts over from its input after a crash.Its own checkpoint can list a rollout as in flight whose result it already has, so after a crash it may run or count that rollout again. A controller that waits for a restart's reply waits until the servers' leases expire, because the restart's next model call waits for resume.
Publishes only after every commit succeeded, then resumes, and calls renew if publishing takes longer than the lease.A published checkpoint that is missing a server's manifest fails at restore with checkpoint_invalid_state, and every continued rollout starts over. A lease that expires makes the server resume on its own, and the controller's next call for that checkpoint is refused with checkpoint_stale.
Records each attempt somewhere that outlives its process before sending it, and after a crash retires the last recorded attempt of every rollout that starts over.A harness that outlived the crash, such as one in a remote sandbox, keeps calling Gym, and the servers accept its calls into the rerun, because the retire marks of the crashed processes are gone. A rollout that continues from the checkpoint needs no such retire: the restore marks the attempt it replaces on every server.
Sends each continued rollout as exactly its next attempt, with the same task, and restores a checkpoint only if no later run sent its rollouts again. A flat row sent through the legacy flat-row wrapper names its attempt either in its rollout ID, as _ng_rollout_id: <id>-aN, or with _ng_attempt_index, never both.A flat row that sets both fails, because its ID would not decode to one rollout and attempt. A different task is refused because the environment server checks each restored episode's task digest. A different attempt number finds no restored state and starts from its input. Restoring after a later run sent the rollouts again installs an attempt next to one that may still be running.
Resumes before it retires a straggler, repeats every call that failed until it succeeds, except a commit refused with checkpoint_export_failed, which it abandons by resuming and preparing again under a new checkpoint ID, forgets rollouts it is finished with, restored ones included, repeats the retire when a forget returns checkpoint_retire_incomplete, deletes checkpoint directories it does not keep, and keeps each group's group attempt.
  • A retire during a checkpoint is refused with checkpoint_invalid_phase.
  • A commit repeated after checkpoint_export_failed is refused again with the same error, so a controller that only repeats it never publishes that checkpoint.
  • A failed retire or forget that is not repeated leaves the attempt's state or its entry on the servers that missed it.
  • Without forget, every server keeps one entry per retired or restored rollout for the rest of the run.
  • A forget refused with checkpoint_retire_incomplete changes nothing, and the retired session behind it holds up every checkpoint until a repeated retire frees it.
  • Unkept directories accumulate.
  • A group whose attempt changed waits for members that never arrive until its verification times out.

What each kind of server must provide

ServerMust provideIf it does not
Environment server protocolDeclares checkpoint_mode = "exported" and records a boundary before each step, naming the sessions the next step reuses. Runs each step as a wait step or a replay step, and uses replay only for steps that are safe to repeat. Chooses session IDs before it starts the sessions. Sends x-ng-agent-activation on every agent run it may invoke again after a restore. Marks its episode as a restart when a session start's reply carries x-ng-checkpoint-restart.A protocol that keeps the default, restart_only, makes every episode a restart, which is correct but repeats work after a crash. A step that is marked replay but changes state runs twice after a restore. Without the activation header, the agent runs a repeated activation as a new one.
Agent server
  • Declares checkpoint_mode = "exported" and implements:
    • export_agent_sessions;
    • restore_agent_sessions, which installs every session or none;
    • retire_agent_session, which tolerates state it already freed.
  • Records a boundary before each model call and after each model response whose tool calls have not run, and wraps each model call so it counts as at the boundary before it.
  • Answers its last finished run with the saved reply.
  • Treats a session start with the same ID and episode as the same session.
  • Sends a rollout ID on every call.
  • Stops, in its restore hook, anything the crashed process left running.
An agent that keeps the default, restart_only, takes part as restart-only, so its rollouts start over after a crash. A boundary in the middle of a tool round saves a conversation that disagrees with the resources server's state. A call without a rollout ID is refused with 400 checkpoint_rollout_id_required, since a checkpoint could neither record nor retire it. A harness that the restore hook leaves running can act on its sandbox alongside the continued attempt.
Resources server
  • Declares:
    • checkpoint_mode as stateless, exported or restart_only, which is the default;
    • checkpoint_verify as replay only if /verify is safe to repeat.
  • In exported mode implements export_session_states, restore_session_states, which installs every session or none, and retire_session_state, which tolerates state it already freed.
  • A retire calls retire_session_state in every mode and the base hook does nothing, so a restart_only or stateless server that keeps per-session state must free it there.
  • Declares every route that starts a session in checkpoint_session_starts: /seed_session by default and /reset for a Gymnasium server.
  • Ends sessions through /close_session, /verify or checkpoint_session_ended.
  • Builds its app through the shared setup, so the checkpoint participant is installed.
  • Deletes what it keeps outside Gym, such as snapshots, once no checkpoint refers to it.
  • A server declared stateless that holds state continues rollouts against state that is missing.
  • Verification wrongly declared safe to repeat repeats its effect.
  • These fail at startup:
    • an exported server without the hooks;
    • a server whose checkpoint_mode or checkpoint_verify is not one of the allowed values.
  • A restart_only or stateless server that keeps per-session state but does not free it in retire_session_state keeps that state after a retire, because the retired session's later requests, such as a terminal step, are refused.
  • A route that starts a session without being declared is not held at admission, so a session it starts during a checkpoint can be missing from the commit.
  • With checkpointing on:
    • a server whose app leaves out the checkpoint participant refuses to start;
    • a session start without a rollout ID is refused with 400 checkpoint_rollout_id_required.
  • Snapshots outside Gym are never freed.
Policy model server
  • The model server that produces training tokens takes part, through checkpoint: {policy: true} in its instance config, with generation_cuts: true to ask its workers for generation cuts.
  • Judge and simulator model servers do not take part and keep serving.
  • Has a capture ledger that can export, import, retire and delete rows, and that implements mark_started() and delete_unstarted().
    • This way policy servers that share the ledger, such as a policy model and its reasoning-off variant, never delete each other's restored rows.
    • Gym's own ledgers implement both.
  • Optionally reaches each inference worker's /ng-control/v1/generation-cut route, through generation_cut_control_url where a backend serves it at another address.
A policy server whose ledger lacks any of these methods fails at startup. Discovery fails when no model server takes part. A worker that cannot cut regenerates its held calls after a restore, which is correct but slower. A judge call made during a verification that runs again is made again, so judge-based verification is safe to repeat only if a second judgment is acceptable.

A server that provides none of this is not an error. Agents without hooks, resources servers in restart_only mode and environment protocols without boundaries take part as restart-only, as rollouts that cannot be saved describes, and their rollouts never hold up a checkpoint.

Other pull requests and components the stack depends on

DependencyWhat the stack relies on it for
Capture ledger and record store retire and delete, NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym#3938 and #3939
  • Retire removes a rollout attempt's ledger and leaves a durable fence, so later rows for that attempt are discarded and capture admission refuses to capture its calls.
  • Reading a retired ledger raises RolloutRetiredError rather than returning an empty manifest.
  • Delete removes the ledger and its fence, so the ID reads as unused again.
  • The policy model participant:
    • retires the ledgers of an attempt when it retires the attempt and when a restore continues it as the next attempt;
    • deletes the ledger of restored state that nothing claimed, so no fence is left for an attempt the controller may still send.
  • #3938 and #3939 have merged, so the checkpoint stack sits on main.
  • The policy model pull request, #3883, adds two ledger methods on top:
    • mark_started(), which a restored attempt's first admitted call uses to create the shared marker <capture key>.lineage.started with O_CREAT|O_EXCL under the rollout's lock;
    • delete_unstarted(), which deletes restored ledgers that no server sharing them has marked.
  • A custom ledger must implement both.
Token-capture builder, already on mainThe builder treats calls with the same parent and the same prompt as retries of one call, and keeps the one a later call extended or the one on the verified final path. This is what makes a model call made again after a restore harmless. A retry of the last call in a rollout can be resolved only through the verified final path; otherwise the builder marks it unresolved, and the consumer masks the rollout rather than train on a generation nobody confirmed.
Agent session lifecycle, NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym#3784, on mainEnvironment servers drive agents through sessions with caller-chosen IDs: a repeated session start with the same ID and request returns the existing session, and close returns the session's observations. A repeated close returns the same receipt only within session_close_retry_window_seconds, so a client must finish retrying a close within that window, and the environment server treats close as a step it waits for and records.
Session routing for several workers, NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym#3905Each session's requests reach the worker that holds it: a routing claim in a directory the workers share names that worker for each session ID, and a request whose worker is gone gets 410. Merged. #3909, also merged, adds the claim rewrite a restore uses.
NeMo RL forget support, NVIDIA-NeMo/RL#4549NeMo RL must call forget once a retired rollout is finished for good, and also once a restored rollout is, because a restore refuses the attempt it replaces exactly as a retire does. Until it does, every Gym server keeps one entry per retired or restored rollout for the whole training run. When a forget returns checkpoint_retire_incomplete, NeMo RL must repeat the retire before it repeats the forget.
uvicorn's worker modelWorkers of one server share a port and are supervised by a main process that serves no requests and hosts the checkpoint coordinator. A worker that loses the coordinator stops itself, and a worker that starts while a checkpoint is open closes at once. If the main process dies, the whole server is down, and the checkpoint fails like any other unreachable participant.
Ray, only for servers that declare ray_enabled = TrueNothing in the checkpoint path uses Ray. A server that keeps session state in Ray tasks or actors must still save and restore it through its own hooks, since the participant only sees what the hooks return.

Environmental assumptions

Gym assumesIf it does not hold
The checkpoint directory is on a filesystem that every Gym server can reach at the same path, and that supports atomic rename, hard links and fsync of files and directories.A server that cannot reach the path, or a filesystem that refuses a hard link, fails the commit with checkpoint_invalid_state, so no checkpoint is published. A filesystem that acknowledges fsync without making the data durable can lose a published checkpoint in a host crash; restore then finds a missing or mismatched file and fails with the same error, and the rollouts start over.
Restore runs into freshly started server processes that have not served any rollout.Each participant refuses the restore: an environment server with live episodes, an agent with live sessions or session starts in progress, a resources server with live sessions or requests in flight, and a policy model that has served calls or lost a worker. Coordination then undoes the restore and the rollouts start over.
Server names and the set of participants are the same at restore as at commit.Each participant reads the directory named after its kind and server name, so a renamed or new server finds no manifest and the restore fails with checkpoint_invalid_state.
One controller at a time, fenced by checkpoint ID.See the controller table above. Fencing covers prepare, commit, restore and resume, and the 64 most recently resumed IDs.
Clocks on the controller's and the servers' machines roughly agree. Every control call carries an absolute deadline in seconds since the Unix epoch, and each server compares it with its own clock; a lease lasts until the deadline plus lease_grace_seconds, 600 seconds by default.A server whose clock runs ahead treats deadlines as passed early and returns checkpoint_deadline_exceeded. One whose clock runs behind keeps working after the controller has given up, which is safe because the controller's repeat gets the remembered result. A skew larger than the lease grace can expire a lease at once, which resumes that server and aborts the checkpoint. Each of these fails closed. Episode deadlines use each process's monotonic clock and are not affected.
  • Session cookies and MCP tokens still verify after a restart.
  • With checkpointing on, an MCP token also names the attempt whose seed minted it. A resources server refuses:
    • a token whose attempt a retire or a restore has marked;
    • a token that names another attempt than its session's;
    • a token that names none.
    So the harness of a replaced attempt cannot keep using its token after a restore; the replacement gets its own token by seeding under its own attempt.
  • An environment server marks an episode that grants MCP access as a restart, so no agent that holds a token is continued past its seed.
  • A direct HTTP grant carries the seeding attempt's rollout prefix, and an agent that continues a session after a restore sends its tool calls under its own activation's prefix.
  • Both are signed with a key derived from the server's class and configured name, so the key is stable as long as those do not change.
  • Session cookies are signed with a timestamp and expire after Starlette's default of 14 days.
A restored session whose cookie or token no longer verifies reaches the server as a request without a session, so it cannot find its restored state. That happens if a server's class or name changes between commit and restore, or if a cookie is older than 14 days when the continued rollout uses it.
No dataset row has an explicit rollout ID that ends in -a<N>, where N is a positive number, such as task-a2. That suffix is reserved: <id>-a<N> always means attempt N of rollout <id>, which is what NeMo RL sends for a restored turn.Rollout collection refuses such a row with an error naming its line when its input or its materialized rows load, so a dataset whose own IDs end this way must rename them. A request body that sets such an ID and also a nonzero _ng_attempt_index is refused, because its ID would not decode to one rollout and attempt.
The control bearer token, checkpoint.control_auth_token, is the same for the controller and every server, and checkpointing is enabled with checkpoint.enabled: true everywhere.Calls with a wrong token are refused with 401 checkpoint_unauthorized, and a server without checkpointing has no control routes, so discovery skips it and its rollouts are not covered.

What the stack deliberately does not handle

Some failures are outside the design, either because another component owns them or because handling them would cost more than the failure. Known gaps describes the open ones in detail.

  • Several Gym deployments sharing one policy model are not supported, and saving the controller's own state is the controller's job.
  • A server that misdeclares what it can save, such as a resources server declared stateless that holds state, is trusted. Gym cannot detect it. A declaration that is not a mode at all, such as a misspelled one, fails at startup.
  • Opaque harnesses saved through sandbox snapshots still need two pieces: a way to tell servers which checkpoints were deleted so they can free snapshots, and a way for a restored harness's pending call to reach the restored servers under the next attempt.
  • A session start sent twice to a server with several workers can leave a copy on another worker until the server restarts.
  • A session start route the server does not declare is not held at admission or tracked, so a server must list every route that starts a session in checkpoint_session_starts. Gym cannot detect an undeclared one.
  • A /run the controller itself sends twice for an attempt is not made idempotent; that is planned as separate work.
  • A crash right after a group's comparison makes the remaining members wait for cohort_collection_timeout_s before they start over.
  • The evaluation controller's dispatch log is not synced to disk. A killed process leaves its lines behind, and a host crash takes the Gym servers on that host down with it, so nothing on that host is left to retire.

Part 2

The v2 design

What this design does

Training and evaluation runs keep thousands of rollouts in flight at once. When the job crashes or is preempted, every one of those rollouts is lost and has to start over from its input. Some rollouts, such as software engineering tasks, run for tens of minutes, so a single preemption can throw away hours of generation.

This design lets whatever process sends rollouts to Gym save the ones in flight and continue them after a crash. That process is called the controller. Gym does not care which program plays the role: a trainer and an evaluation run use the same calls and get the same guarantees.

Four rules carry the design.

  • Each rollout records a safe point after every step it completes, and a checkpoint saves it at the latest one, so nothing is ever saved halfway through a step.
  • Each run of a rollout carries an attempt number, so after a crash the saved rollout continues as its next attempt and Gym can refuse anything the old attempt still sends.
  • Every environment server, agent, resources server and the policy model server takes part in every checkpoint, while judge and simulator model servers keep serving.
    • A rollout that touches a server unable to save its state is simply left out: it keeps running, and if a crash does happen it starts over.
  • Gym checkpoints its servers in a fixed order of its own, so the controller asks for one checkpoint and never sequences servers itself.

In a test deployment on one workstation, 16,000 rollouts with about 12,000 in flight were prepared in 3.6 to 7.6 seconds, written in 1.8 to 4.6 seconds and restored in 3.2 to 5.0 seconds, and every saved rollout finished after the restore.

What the design must guarantee

The requirements are listed in priority order, and when two of them conflict the earlier one wins.

  1. A continued rollout behaves as if it was never interrupted. It sees the same state and continues the same token lineage, and no step runs twice unless that step has been declared safe to repeat. When Gym cannot guarantee this for a rollout, it restarts the rollout from its input instead.
  2. Every piece of checkpoint state has an end of life. Each piece is freed by an explicit event, such as a retire or a later commit, so nothing grows with the length of the run and nothing waits for a restart or a timeout to be cleaned up.
  3. A rollout that cannot be saved never stops the others from being saved.
  4. Checkpoints are fast enough to run often. Tens of thousands of rollouts in flight should take seconds, so checkpoints can run on a timer and right before a preemption.
  5. The design has as few moving parts as the requirements above allow. There is no acknowledgement protocol, no background sweep, and no state shared between servers.
  6. Nothing changes when checkpointing is off. Unless the configuration's checkpoint: block sets enabled: true, no server installs any checkpoint route or behavior.

Two things are out of scope. Gym does not support several Gym deployments sharing one policy model, and saving the controller's own state, such as a trainer's, is the controller's job.

Terms used in this design

Later sections use each of these terms only in the sense given here.

ControllerThe process that sends rollouts to Gym and decides when to checkpoint, such as a trainer or an evaluation run.
Rollout and attemptA rollout has a stable ID, and each run of it is an attempt numbered from 0. r-a1 means attempt 1 of rollout r. The suffix -a<N> is reserved for this, so a rollout's own ID never ends in it.
ParticipantThe part of one Gym server that owns state a checkpoint must save. The four kinds are environment, policy model, agent and resources.
BoundaryThe safe point an episode records after each step it completes, naming the next step and what that step needs.
Wait step and replay stepA step still running when a checkpoint starts. The checkpoint waits for a wait step to finish, while a replay step simply runs again after a crash, so it must be safe to repeat.
Checkpoint modeWhat a server's code can save, declared as checkpoint_mode on its class: restart_only, the default, saves nothing and its rollouts restart; stateless, for resources servers only, holds nothing a continuation needs; exported saves and restores its state through its kind's hooks.
UnclaimedRestored state that no run of the next attempt has used yet. A commit whose scope leaves its rollout out deletes it.
Continue and restartAfter a crash, a saved rollout continues from its boundary as its next attempt, while a rollout that was not saved restarts from its input as its next attempt.
PrepareStops each server from admitting new work and waits until every rollout in flight sits at a boundary, or reports the ones that cannot be saved.
CommitWrites each server's state for the rollouts the controller will continue into the checkpoint directory.
ResumeReopens every server after a checkpoint. It also cancels a checkpoint that was not finished, so it doubles as the abort.
RestoreInstalls a checkpoint's state into fresh server processes after a crash, so each saved rollout can continue as its next attempt.
RetireAbandons an attempt: every server marks it, so its late requests are refused from then on, stops its work, and frees its state.
ForgetTells every server that a retired or restored rollout is finished for good, so it can drop the entry it kept to refuse that rollout's late requests.

Components and what each owns

Select a component to see what it owns, what it checkpoints, and what it never does.

One checkpoint from start to finish

The controller sends rollouts to environment servers as usual. For checkpoints it calls Gym's coordination functions, which in turn call every participant, so the controller never talks to an individual server.

Rollouts flow through environment servers, and checkpoint calls flow through coordination.

A checkpoint, followed later by a crash, unfolds in five stages:

  1. The controller stops sending rollouts and calls prepare. Each participant stops admitting new work, and each episode in flight finishes its current step if it is a wait step and then stops at its next boundary.
  2. When prepare returns, every participant has reported whether it is ready and has listed the rollouts in flight that it cannot save. Those rollouts are called restarts.
  3. The controller calls commit with the rollouts it will continue, leaving the restarts out, and every participant writes its records followed by a manifest that names them.
  4. The controller saves its own checkpoint, recording which rollouts continue and which restart, and only then calls resume so everything carries on.
  5. If Gym crashes later, fresh Gym processes start and the controller calls restore and then resume. It retires each restart's old attempt and sends every rollout again as its next attempt, so saved rollouts continue where they stopped and restarts begin from their input.

Step through the lifecycle

Pick a scenario and step through it. In the diagram, the current step's messages are drawn at full strength; earlier steps are faded. The boxes under the diagram show each component's state after the step; a thick solid border marks a change and a dashed border marks a problem state. The scenarios use a training framework as the controller; rollout collection plays the same part in evaluation runs.

    State machines in the walkthrough

    Every participant runs the same control-phase machine. Agent sessions, policy calls, and episodes have their own small machines. While a scenario plays, the machine that the current step affects highlights its current state with a thick solid border.

    The state machine every server runs

    Every participant runs the same control code, reached through bearer-protected routes under /ng-control/v1/checkpoint. This shared code, the control plane, tracks which phase the participant is in, which checkpoint is active, how long the controller's lease lasts and how state is written, so each kind of server only has to describe its own state.

    The phases of one participant. Retire and forget are accepted only in idle and restored.

    Rules that keep the phases safe

    Only one checkpoint can be active at a time, and a call naming a different checkpoint ID is refused with checkpoint_conflict. Once a checkpoint has been resumed it can never come back: resume records the checkpoint's ID, so a delayed call from an old controller cannot reopen or overwrite anything. Gym keeps the last 64 resumed IDs, which is enough to catch stale calls while keeping the record small.

    A controller that disappears cannot leave Gym closed either. Every call renews a lease that lasts until the call's deadline plus lease_grace_seconds (600 seconds by default), and when the lease expires the participant resumes on its own, which is the same as cancelling the checkpoint. If reopening fails for any reason, it tries again.

    Every finished call can be repeated safely.

    • A repeated commit returns the same reply as the first, so the controller can retry any call with the same checkpoint ID without worrying about what already happened.
    • A repeated commit that finds its manifest already published also syncs the participant's directory before it reports success. A commit that reports success is therefore durable even if the write that published the manifest failed before syncing it.
    • Before writing anything, commit checks that the participant is still ready. If something changed since prepare and the participant's export has not started, the commit fails with 409 checkpoint_export_failed, so Gym never writes a state that is no longer consistent.
    • An export that fails ends the checkpoint the same way.
      • On a server with several workers, the export fails when a worker was lost after the readiness check and before the snapshot, because that worker took its records with it.
    • Every later commit for that checkpoint ID is refused with the same error, because a second export could take a later cut than the other participants committed. The controller resumes and prepares again under a new checkpoint ID.

    The order Gym checkpoints servers in

    The order in which servers are prepared, resumed and retired matters for correctness, and it depends on which Gym server calls which, so Gym fixes it rather than leaving it to the controller. The coordination functions keep no state between calls, which lets the controller call and retry them freely.

    CallOrderReason
    prepareEnvironment servers, then the policy model, then agents, then resources servers, each stage ready before the next starts.Environment servers stop their episodes first. The policy model then holds its responses, so agents waiting on it reach a boundary, and resources servers go last because agents keep calling them until they stop.
    resumeThe reverse.No server reopens before the servers it calls.
    commit and restoreAll servers at once.By then every server is stopped at a consistent point, so writing is independent.
    retire and forgetEnvironment servers, then agents, then the policy model and resources servers together.A caller stops before the servers it calls, so nothing upstream sends new work for the attempt.

    None of these calls is atomic across servers

    Each coordination call reaches every server separately, so a call can succeed on some servers and fail on others. What makes this safe is that every call can be repeated with the same ID, and that a partly finished call never produces a state the controller would act on. The table below says what each call leaves behind when it fails partway, and what the controller does about it.

    CallAfter a partial failureWhat the controller does
    prepareSome servers are prepared and others are still preparing, with admission closed on all of them.Calls resume, which reopens every server, and tries again later.
    commitSome servers have written their records and manifest, and others have not. The checkpoint is not valid yet, because the controller has not published it.Repeats the commit, which reuses each server's single write, or resumes without publishing.
    • If a server's export failed, every repeat fails with 409 checkpoint_export_failed: that checkpoint is over, and the controller resumes and prepares again under a new checkpoint ID. Causes include:
      • one of its workers was lost before the snapshot;
      • the server was no longer ready before its export started.
    • A repeated commit must name the same directory and episodes; one that names others is refused, since the write belongs to the first.
    • A directory from a commit that was never published is the controller's to delete along with any other checkpoint it does not keep.
    resumeSome servers are open and others are still closed until their lease expires.Repeats resume. A server that already resumed recognizes the checkpoint ID and returns at once. A server still deleting restored state that the commit left out stays closed until the deletion finishes, because a new attempt of that rollout may start there; if the deadline passes first, it reports the deadline and keeps its phase for the repeated resume. A server whose failed restore could not reopen admission is reopened by the next resume under any checkpoint ID, after any install that outlived that restore finishes within the resume's deadline.
    restoreSome servers have installed state and others have not.Nothing: coordination undoes it on its own by retiring the new attempts on every server, which frees what was installed, then resuming every server and reporting the error. The controller starts those rollouts over from their input. Every server the restore reached keeps refusing the attempts it replaces until the controller forgets those rollouts.
    retireStages run in order, so a failure stops the call: earlier stages have retired the attempt and later stages may still be running its work.Repeats the retire until it succeeds. A server that already finished finds nothing left to stop and returns at once, and the refusal it recorded stays in place either way. A policy call that was waiting at closed admission when the attempt was marked stays refused, even after forget. The refusal is recorded before any work the deadline limits, so a server that received the retire too late to stop anything still refuses the attempts.
    forgetSome servers have dropped the entry and others still hold it. A server whose retire has not yet freed every session of the rollout refuses forget and changes nothing. That includes a session that a session start registered after the retire, and a session start of a retired attempt that is still in flight.Repeats the forget, after repeating the retire if a server refused it. Until then the remaining servers only keep refusing requests that should never come.

    Restore is therefore the only call with built-in undo. Every other call relies on the controller repeating it, and the controller rules require exactly that.

    How episodes are saved

    The environment server runs the episode protocol, so it is the one that records where each episode can continue. The main protocol today, single_agent_turn, runs five stages with one agent and records a boundary before each of them. A protocol with several agents would record boundaries in the same way, with each boundary naming every session it needs.

    StageStep typeReason
    Start the resources and agent sessionsReplayStarting a session with a caller-chosen session ID can safely run twice.
    Run the agentReplayThe agent stops at its own turn boundaries and continues from them.
    Close the agent sessionWaitClosing returns the agent's observations only once.
    VerifyWhatever the resources server reported when its session startedOnly the resources server knows whether its verification can run twice.
    Return the resultBoundary onlyThe result is recorded, so a restore never verifies twice.
