    The states of one episode inside the environment server. Time an episode spends stopped for a checkpoint does not count against its deadline.

    Every episode in flight can be saved. An episode that has not reached its first boundary yet is saved with an empty boundary and starts over from its input after a crash, while a restored episode stays at the boundary it was restored from until it records a new one.

    The subtle case is a replay step that ends while a checkpoint is open. The checkpoint has already counted the episode at the boundary before that step, so the step's result must not move the saved boundary. Instead the result waits at the next boundary until resume, and the saved boundary and the episode's real progress never disagree.

    A replay step that fails while a checkpoint is open does not hold up the checkpoint either.

    • The episode's boundary is cleared, so the checkpoint saves it with an empty boundary. After a crash it starts over from its input instead of continuing past a step that failed.
    • The episode stops at that cleared boundary until resume, where it counts as stopped rather than as a blocker.
    • Only after resume does the step's error reach the episode, so its cleanup, which may close its sessions, and its /run reply both wait for resume.
    • The episode therefore cannot end while Gym is prepared:
      • its sessions stay as the checkpoint saw them;
      • its rollout is still in flight for the controller, which names it in the commit.

    The legacy flat-row wrapper, which turns a flat row into a request on the typed single_agent_turn request path, reads a row's rollout and attempt the way the agent does.

    • An explicit rollout ID that ends in -aN, such as r-a1, is attempt N of rollout r.
    • A row without that suffix takes its attempt from _ng_attempt_index.
    • A continued rollout sent again as a flat row therefore finds its restored episode and continues from its boundary.
    • The suffix is reserved for this:
      • rollout collection refuses a dataset row whose explicit ID ends in -a<N> with an error when its input or its materialized rows load, so a dataset whose own IDs end that way must rename them;
      • a body that sets such an ID and also a nonzero _ng_attempt_index is refused.

    How the policy model avoids waiting

    A generation can take minutes, so the checkpoint never waits for one to finish. This is safe because of a simple fact about agents: an agent waiting for a model response is still at the boundary it recorded before making the call. If the call is made again after a crash, the continued rollout matches its saved state exactly.

    One model call across a checkpoint. A call that arrives while a checkpoint is open waits outside the gate, so prepare never counts it, and its caller is still at the boundary it recorded before the call.

    Calls that have not been delivered are left out

    When admission closes, the model holds every response that has not started streaming, and the checkpoint leaves those calls out. After a crash the agent simply makes the call again. Only a response that is already streaming has to finish before prepare is ready.

    A response starts streaming with its first chunk of answer data, not with its headers.

    • A streaming response sends its headers before it reads its body, and the model server sends keep-alive comments while the backend is still generating.
    • If either counted as the start:
      • prepare would wait for a call that has produced nothing instead of cutting it;
      • a call whose last token write the checkpoint is holding could never finish, so prepare would stall.
    • So:
      • headers, empty chunks and keep-alive comments leave the call cuttable;
      • its first answer chunk is held while admission is closed;
      • an answer that already started still drains before prepare completes.

    A call's row in the capture ledger is published when its response starts, not when the inference worker has staged its tokens.

    • The ledger is the record the checkpoint copies, so it must hold exactly the answers callers received.
    • If rows were written at staging, an undelivered call would already have a row, and the checkpoint would have to find and drop it. That fails in two ways:
      • Several policy servers can share one run-wide ledger, and a server cannot see the calls another server is holding, so it would export their rows.
      • A call admitted just before admission closed may not have its capture identity yet when the commit takes its snapshot, so its row could land after the snapshot and before the export reads the ledger.
    • Publishing at the first answer chunk removes both: an undelivered call has no row.
    • The write happens after the response is allowed to start and before the chunk is sent.
      • A cancellation cannot cut it short, so a retire or a checkpoint waits for it.
      • If it fails, the call is recorded as failed and no answer is sent.
    • A call that leaves before its response starts has no row and is simply made again.
    • Every model server that writes the ledger must be behind the checkpoint gate. With checkpointing on, a model server named by an agent with token capture that is not a checkpoint policy server stops the run at startup.

    A waiting call of a retired attempt stays refused

    A call that waits at closed admission has not been admitted, so a retire marks it directly. Once its attempt is marked retired, the call is refused for good: it stays refused after the controller forgets the rollout, and even if the retire was cut short by its deadline. The retire returns only after every such waiting call has left, so a forget that follows cannot let one in.

    Generation cuts save compute but are never required

    With generation cuts turned on, prepare also asks each inference worker to save the tokens it has generated so far for each held call. After a crash, the repeated call continues from that saved prefix, called a cut, instead of generating it again.

    • A cut is only an optimization, so a call the worker could not cut is generated again, which is always correct.
    • A call restored with a cut keeps that cut until it delivers its response, so a retry can continue it.
    • After each cut round, the newest cut of the call replaces that restored cut, because the new checkpoint keeps only the newest cut's staged rows. A retry never receives a cut whose staged rows may already be deleted.
    • With several workers, a worker claims a restored cut before the call runs and never gives back one the call used, so a retry of that call is generated again instead.
    • The cut request gets half of the time left for prepare, so a stuck worker cannot use up the time the later stages need.
    • A call with constrained decoding is never cut and never continues one, since a token prefix cannot restore its structured decoder.

    Some inference backends, such as Megatron inference, take cuts at a different address from their OpenAI API. Each of them lists a generation_cut_control_url, and once those addresses are set, a backend without one fails its cut rather than guessing where to send it.

    Token lineage continues under the next attempt

    Restore imports the capture ledger's rows under the next attempt's capture key, so the repeated call finds its parent through normal fingerprint matching without any extra header.

    A model server restores only into a fresh process

    A model server that has already served a call refuses to restore, because a ledger it wrote might belong to a live episode. With several workers, restore is also refused once any worker has left, since its replacement cannot report what the old worker served.

    Policy servers that share a capture ledger keep each other's restored rows

    Several policy model servers can capture into one ledger, for example a policy model and its reasoning-off variant.

    • A restored attempt may call only one of them. Each server's commit deletes the restored attempts that its scope leaves out and that no call has reached on that server.
    • Without coordination, the server the attempt never called would delete the ledger the other server is continuing.
    • So the first call of a restored attempt that a server admits creates a shared started marker, <capture key>.lineage.started, before the call can write a row or be held.
      • The marker is created with O_CREAT|O_EXCL under the rollout's lock.
      • The deletion takes the same lock and skips every attempt that has one.
      • Checking for rows instead would not be enough, because a call held for the checkpoint has written no row yet.
    • The marker ends with the attempt's ledger, whether that ledger is retired, deleted, or cleared by a later restore.
    • It is not synced to disk:
      • the other servers only need to see it;
      • after a crash the next step is a restore, which deletes every marker the dead execution left;
      • syncing would cost one directory sync per restored rollout in a burst right after resume.

    The deletion removes the ledger before the server drops its own record of the restored attempt. If removing the ledger fails, the attempt is still unclaimed, and a repeated commit deletes it again instead of leaving the ledger behind.

    Ledger cleanup waits for resume

    The controller removes old capture ledgers through retire and delete routes on the model server. Those routes answer 409 while a checkpoint is open, because commit reads the ledger of every continued rollout.

    How agents are saved

    An agent that implements the session hooks saves each session at its latest turn-loop boundary. Simple Agent, the one Gym ships today, records a boundary before each model call and another after each model response whose tool calls have not run yet. The hooks hand the session's state to the checkpoint and rebuild it after a restore, and they are asynchronous and take every session at once, so an agent that keeps state outside its process can save all of it concurrently.

    The states of one agent session. A session waiting for a model response counts as stopped at its last boundary, and stays there if the response arrives while a checkpoint is open.

    Whether an agent can be saved depends on whether it implements the hooks, not on how its harness is built. An opaque harness can be saved if it runs in a sandbox that can snapshot its whole runtime, for example one backed by a microVM: the agent's hooks pause the sandbox and save a reference to its snapshot, and after a crash they resume that snapshot. Two pieces of that path are still open, and the known gaps describe them. An agent without hooks is treated as one that cannot be saved, and its rollouts restart.

    A model call made during a checkpoint waits at the policy model until resume, and one already being generated has its response held, so the agent stays at the boundary before the call.

    • A response the model finished sending just before it prepared can still reach the agent while the checkpoint is open. The agent then holds it and stays at that boundary until resume, so the session never starts running again in the middle of a checkpoint.
    • The model has already recorded that call. If Gym crashes before resume:
      • the restored agent makes the call again from the same boundary;
      • the token-capture builder treats the two calls like a client retry: it keeps the one the agent continued from.

    The environment server records the step before it invokes an agent, so its checkpoint can still have a run ahead of it while the agent's checkpoint already has that run finished. Runs are therefore idempotent. The environment server numbers each run of a session, and the agent saves the reply of its last finished run with the session. When a restored environment server invokes a run the agent already finished, the agent answers with the saved reply instead of running it again, so no model or tool call is repeated.

    A legacy /run, where the agent drives the whole episode itself, is tracked as an episode of its own: its session start and turn loop are replay steps, and its verification uses the step type the resources server reported. Finally, each run of a session reports its observations under its own invocation ID, and the session's saved state includes how many runs it has started, so a restored session's next run takes the next ID while a continued run keeps the one it already had.

    How resources servers declare their state

    Each resources server states in its code how its sessions are saved. This is a class attribute rather than a configuration setting, because only the server's author knows whether its state can be saved, and a setting could claim support the code does not have.

    The three modes. A server nobody has reviewed falls back to restarting its rollouts.

    The server learns each session's lifetime from requests it already serves, so no route has to be labelled as a change or a read.

    • A successful session start, /seed_session or another route the server declares, such as a Gymnasium /reset, ties the session to the episode named in the request's rollout path.
    • A /close_session or /verify ends it.
    • Every declared start passes the same admission check before its handler runs: while a checkpoint is open it waits for resume, in every mode, so no session can begin after a commit has fixed its scope.
    • A start without a rollout path is refused, because a session that names no episode could be neither saved nor retired.
    • A resources server that builds its own app instead of the shared one would skip all of this, so with checkpointing on it refuses to start.

    Requests already running finish before the server's state is saved: prepare is ready only once nothing is in flight, and a session start in progress counts too, so the saved sessions always match the environment server's boundary. A request that arrives while a checkpoint is open waits for resume instead of being refused. Only a rollout that keeps running through the checkpoint sends such a request, since a rollout that will be continued has already stopped at a boundary, and refusing it would show a tool error to the model in a third-party harness.

    The reply to /seed_session tells the caller two things without another request: x-ng-checkpoint-verify says whether /verify can run twice, and x-ng-checkpoint-restart says the server cannot save this session. Saved state is written exactly as the server holds it, keeping dictionary key order, NaN and infinities, because tool outputs often serialize stored state and a restored session must answer exactly as the original would.

    • A restart_only server lists the episode of every session start still in flight as a restart, because that start's reply will carry x-ng-checkpoint-restart and prepare does not wait for it.
    • The server records a session's start or end as soon as its response starts, before the reply is sent. A client that disconnects while the reply is on its way cannot cancel the request before the change is recorded.
    • A /close_session is accepted even from a retired attempt, on purpose, because it is how the server frees that session's state.
    • checkpoint_mode and checkpoint_verify are checked when the server starts, so a misspelled value fails startup instead of acting as a mode of its own.

    A retire calls retire_session_state for each retired session in every mode, not only in exported mode. The base hook does nothing, so a restart_only or stateless server that keeps per-session state must free it there: the retired session's later requests, a terminal step among them, are refused, and nothing else would free it.

    A retire waits for the session starts of its attempts that are already in flight, so it frees the sessions they create.

    • A session start can still finish after its attempt was retired, for example when the retire was cut short while it waited. Its session is then a retired session:
      • its requests are refused;
      • it is never exported;
      • it holds up every checkpoint until a repeated retire frees it.
    • Forget is refused with checkpoint_retire_incomplete while such a session start is in flight or such a session is not yet freed, because forgetting would make the session live again.
    • A retire also does not wait for a protocol route, such as a Gymnasium /reset, that was admitted before the retire and starts its session after the retire returned.
      • That session lands as a retired session too, and forget returns checkpoint_retire_incomplete until a repeated retire frees it.
      • This is safe, but it costs the controller another retire round.

    Rollouts that cannot be saved

    A rollout can only be saved if every server it uses can save its part. When one of them cannot, because it is an agent without session hooks or a resources server in restart_only mode, the rollout is a restart. Earlier versions of this design made a restart block every checkpoint until the controller retired it, which meant one such rollout in flight stopped every other environment in the run from being saved and threw away its own progress at each checkpoint even when nothing crashed. A restart now flows through the checkpoint without stopping anything:

    How a restart is found, reported, left out of the checkpoint, and recovered after a crash.

    The design still fails closed if a controller ignores the restart list. Each participant checks the commit's list against its own restarts and refuses a commit that names one with checkpoint_restart_in_scope, so such a controller gets a failed checkpoint rather than a rollout that is only partly saved.

    The restart list also never changes while a checkpoint is open. An episode is marked as a restart only after any open checkpoint ends, and session starts on servers that cannot save state wait for resume as well. The random sequence tests found why this matters: a session start whose reply arrived in the middle of a checkpoint used to change the list after the state had been written, and the commit then failed.

    The controller does not wait for a restart either. A restart is never in the commit's scope, so it keeps running through the checkpoint, and the controller waits only for /run replies of rollouts that are neither in the commit nor restarts.

    After a crash, the retire that comes before the rerun is what protects it. A harness can run in a remote sandbox that survives the crash, and if it kept calling Gym, its calls would mix into the new attempt's data. The retire makes every server refuse them. An environment protocol that records no boundaries at all treats every episode as a restart, which is why nemo_user_sim episodes no longer block checkpoints.

    How Gym abandons an attempt

    The controller abandons an attempt by calling retire, and every participant handles it the same way, callers first. It marks the rollout as retired up to that attempt, stops the attempt's work and waits until that work has ended, frees the attempt's state, and only then replies.

    The entry lasts exactly as long as a late request can still arrive.

    The entry exists because of late requests. A request that a caller sent just before its own retire travels on a different connection than the retire itself, so it can reach a server after that server has already finished retiring the attempt. Without the entry, the server would accept it and write its rows into the capture files. The entry is a single item per rollout that never moves to a lower attempt and survives even a failed retire, and the controller deletes it with forget once nothing of the rollout can still run.

    The entry is recorded before anything the retire's deadline limits, on every worker of the server as well, so a retire that arrives after its deadline still leaves it and its repeat stops the work. A restore leaves the same entry for each attempt it replaces, as how a checkpoint is restored describes, and that entry also ends only through forget.

    A retire is refused while a checkpoint is open, because stopping an episode waits for its final cleanup while that cleanup's own calls wait for resume, and the retire would wait forever. To give up on a straggler, the controller therefore resumes first, retires it, and then prepares again. A retire that runs out of time is safe to repeat: the episode stays tracked until its task has ended, blocks the next checkpoint in the meantime, and a second retire waits for it again without cancelling the work twice.

    On the policy model, retiring attempt N:

    1. cancels the calls of attempts 0 to N, each only once, so a repeated retire waits for a cleanup the first one started instead of interrupting it;
    2. waits for them;
    3. retires their capture ledgers in one batch.
    • Calls of those attempts that are still waiting at closed admission are refused for good, even after forget and even if the retire is cut short. The retire returns only after they have left.
    • On a resources server, a session start that finishes after its attempt was retired leaves a retired session that a repeated retire frees, as how resources servers declare their state describes.

    A retire stops its episodes concurrently, up to a fixed number at a time, so one large retire neither runs one episode after another nor floods the workers and servers it calls. Since retiring an attempt also stops the earlier ones, each rollout is stopped once, through the latest attempt the retire names. A commit deletes the restored state its scope leaves out in the same way. The reply carries only retired_count, the number of distinct attempts named, rather than every ID.

    How a checkpoint is written

    Each participant writes one directory per checkpoint, holding a records file and a manifest that names it. The checkpoint counts only once every participant has written its manifest and the controller has published its own checkpoint.

    State is taken once per checkpoint, and resume and publishing share one lock.

    Each checkpoint takes its state once and writes it once.

    • The writing runs in a thread, which a deadline cannot stop, so the control plane keeps hold of that one write:
      • a repeated commit waits for it;
      • if storing failed, the repeated commit stores the same records again.
    • If the export itself failed, or the participant was no longer ready before its export started, the checkpoint is over:
      • every commit for that checkpoint ID is refused with 409 checkpoint_export_failed;
      • the controller resumes and prepares again under a new checkpoint ID.
    • A checkpoint's saved state therefore can never change between attempts to commit it.
    • What a participant exports is limited to live records inside the commit's scope: the episodes and sessions the scope names that are neither retired nor restarts, plus restored state the scope still continues.

    No manifest can appear after resume has returned. The writer checks a stop flag before each record, and its last check, the rename of its records file and the creation of the manifest all happen under a lock that resume also takes. Two writers can never leave mismatched files either, because the records file is named after its content hash and the manifest is only ever created, never replaced. If two writers race, exactly one publishes and the other removes its own records file.

    A committed manifest also survives a host crash.

    • Before it publishes the manifest, each commit syncs the parent of every directory from the participant's directory up to the controller's checkpoint directory, so a crash cannot lose a directory entry under the manifest.
    • It syncs all of them, not only the ones it created, because an earlier write that failed, or another participant, may have created a directory without syncing its parent.
    • A repeated commit that finds its manifest already published syncs the participant's directory before it reports success, because the write that published the manifest may have failed before syncing it.
    • A commit that reports success is therefore always durable.

    Saved state reads back exactly as it was written.

    • Records keep every dictionary's key order, NaN and infinities.
    • Gym checks opaque state once to confirm it is JSON before writing it unchanged, using orjson for the check and strict JSON as the fallback.
    • A value that would not read back the same fails the commit with an error naming the rollout.
    • Only the commit checks: records that a restore reads back, or that a server's workers pass to each other, were parsed from JSON, so they are not checked again.
    • Records are encoded, hashed and written one at a time and read back the same way:
      • neither commit nor restore ever holds a whole records file in memory;
      • restore keeps only the records it will install while still verifying the whole file.

    How a checkpoint is restored

    Restore runs in fresh processes after a crash. Each participant stops admitting work, reads and verifies its records, and installs the ones the controller continues under the next attempt. It then waits for the controller's resume before admitting any of those attempts, and each restored record stays until its new attempt actually starts.

    A restore also refuses the attempts it replaces.

    • Before any work its deadline limits, every participant, and every worker of each participant, marks each episode in the restore's scope as retired up to that attempt, whether or not the restore then succeeds.
    • A harness of the replaced attempt that outlived the crash, for example in a remote sandbox, is then refused with 409 checkpoint_stale_attempt by the restored servers instead of writing into the continued rollout.
    • These marks end only when the controller forgets the rollout, so the controller forgets every restored rollout once it is finished for good, just as it forgets retired ones.

    Before installing anything, a restore removes what earlier failed runs left behind.

    • Suppose a continued rollout made model calls and Gym crashed again before the next checkpoint. Restoring the same checkpoint again deletes everything those runs left for the target attempt and every later attempt, including ledgers, token records and retire fences.
    • A fence left in place would otherwise silently drop the restored rollout's rows.
    • To make this possible, each participant is told every rollout the restore continues, including ones it holds no record of, so a participant that keeps files per rollout can clear them too.
    • A restore that runs out of time reopens admission only once its install has finished, and the retire that cleans up a failed restore waits for the install as well.
    • If a failed restore cannot reopen admission, the participant stays closed.
      • The next resume, under any checkpoint ID, tries the reopen again instead of answering that there is nothing to resume.
      • That resume first waits, within its own deadline, for an install that outlived the restore.
    • Restored state that no new attempt ever uses is not kept forever:
      • the next checkpoint saves it again for as long as the commit names the rollout;
      • the first commit that leaves it out deletes it, without a mark or a ledger fence, because the controller may still start that rollout over as the same attempt.

    Servers with several workers

    Production servers run several uvicorn workers that share one port. A checkpoint call reaches whichever worker accepts the connection, while a session's state lives only in the worker that created it. Two mechanisms make such a server behave as a single participant.

    On the left, one participant for the whole server. On the right, requests reaching the worker that holds their session, as its routing claim names.

    A coordinator in the server's main process owns the participant.

    • Each worker reports to it over a local socket, and it tells every worker when to close, reopen, retire, save and install.
    • Prepare is ready only once every worker is.
    • The checkpoint waits until resume, because what that worker held is unknown, when:
      • fewer workers have registered than configured;
      • a worker is lost while a checkpoint is open.
    • A worker lost after the commit checked readiness but before the snapshot is caught as well: the snapshot asks every worker for its records and fails unless every expected worker answers, so the commit fails with 409 checkpoint_export_failed.

    Session requests find their worker through the session's routing claim.

    • The router reads the session ID the client already sends, from the session cookie, the MCP session token, or the body of a session start or close.
    • The claim, a file in a directory the server's workers share, names the worker that holds the session.
      • A session start claims its session before it runs.
      • Another request claims a session only if its handler used it.
    • A request whose worker is gone gets a 410 instead of running against empty state.
    • The number of workers may change between a checkpoint and its restore: restored sessions are installed on live workers, and the restore rewrites each one's claim to name its new worker, in batches off the event loop.
    • Every worker's restarts reach the coordinator, which combines them into its own report, so a commit that names any worker's restart is refused with checkpoint_restart_in_scope.

    Rewards computed over a group

    GenRM comparison scores each rollout against the other rollouts for the same prompt. Each member's /verify waits inside the resources server until the whole group has arrived, and the server then compares them all and answers every member at once. The server is declared stateless with verification that may run twice, because the group lives in memory, keyed by the group ID and group attempt the caller sends, and there is nothing per session to save.

    The checkpoint must not wait for a member's verification, because that verification waits for other members that may still be generating while generation is paused for the checkpoint, and the two would wait for each other forever. A member waiting in verification is therefore saved at the boundary before verification. After a crash, every member that had not recorded its reward verifies again and the group forms again in the new process, provided the controller keeps each group's group attempt unchanged.

    One crash timing is slow but still correct. If Gym crashes just after a group's comparison, when some members have recorded their reward and others have not, the remaining members wait for members that will never verify again. They fail after cohort_collection_timeout_s, 30 minutes by default, and then restart from their input.

    Situations a real run hits

    Each situation below has a test that fails without the behavior described.

    When the controller or a deadline fails

    If prepare runs out of time, it returns the rollouts that are still blocking and leaves admission closed. The controller then resumes, retires those rollouts and prepares again, so Gym never writes a checkpoint that is only partly consistent. If the controller itself crashes in the middle of a checkpoint, each participant's lease expires and it resumes on its own, so Gym never stays closed waiting for a controller that is gone. A participant whose lease expired keeps trying to reopen after any error, not only after a deadline passed, because nothing else may be left to reopen it.

    When a write fails or races with resume

    • A commit repeated after its write failed stores the same state again and returns the same reply, since the state was taken only once.
    • If the earlier write had already published the manifest and failed before syncing the directory, the repeat syncs the directory before it reports success, so a commit that reports success survives a host crash.
    • If resume arrives while a manifest is being written, it waits for the write's lock. Once resume returns no manifest can appear, so the controller's view and the files on disk never disagree.
    • A commit whose export failed, or whose participant was no longer ready before its export started, ends that checkpoint:
      • every repeat is refused with 409 checkpoint_export_failed;
      • the controller resumes and prepares again under a new checkpoint ID, because a second export could take a later cut than the other participants committed.

    When work finishes or arrives at an awkward moment

    • An episode that finishes during prepare stops at its final boundary with its result instead of replying, so the result cannot be lost between Gym's commit and the controller's own checkpoint.
    • A replay step that ends while a checkpoint is open keeps its result until resume, leaving the saved boundary where it was.
      • One that fails is saved with an empty boundary, so after a crash its episode starts over from its input.
      • It also waits at that boundary until resume, and its cleanup and /run reply wait with it, so the episode cannot finish while Gym is prepared.
    • A client that disconnects from a resources server while a session start or close reply is on its way cannot lose the change, because the server records it when the response starts.
    • A model call that is still generating has its response held and its rows left out. After a crash the agent makes it again, possibly continuing a cut prefix, which matches the saved state because the agent was saved before the call.
    • An agent run that finishes while the environment server's checkpoint still has it ahead is answered again from the agent's saved reply after a restore.

    When a rollout cannot be saved

    A rollout that touches a server unable to save it is listed as a restart, left out of the checkpoint and allowed to keep running while every other rollout is saved.

    • Neither the saved state nor the restart list changes while the checkpoint is open:
      • if its session start reports this in the middle of a checkpoint, the episode is marked only after the checkpoint ends;
      • session starts on such servers wait for resume.
    • The controller never waits for a restart's reply: the restart keeps running through the checkpoint, and after a crash it starts over from its input.
    • No part of a restart is ever written:
      • a session start still in flight on a restart_only server already counts as a restart;
      • every participant exports only live records inside the commit's scope.
    • Coordination also hands every later prepare stage the restarts that earlier stages reported. A participant that cannot tell on its own that an episode is a restart, such as an agent serving an episode that a restart-only resources server or an MCP grant made a restart, does not wait for it either.

    When an attempt is abandoned

    • A request that arrives after its attempt was retired is refused with 409 checkpoint_stale_attempt until the controller forgets the rollout, so late requests can never mix rows into a later attempt.
      • The one request still accepted is a resources session close, which frees the session's state.
    • A restore leaves the same refusal for the attempts it replaces, so a harness that outlived a crash, for example in a remote sandbox, is refused by the restored servers as well.
    • A retire that runs out of time leaves the episode tracked, blocking the next checkpoint until a repeated retire finishes it, so an episode that is only partly stopped is never saved.
    • A model call that was waiting at closed admission when its attempt was retired stays refused, even after forget and even if the retire was cut short.
    • A resources session start that finishes after its attempt was retired registers a retired session. It is refused, never exported and holds up checkpoints until a repeated retire frees it, and forget is refused until then.

    When a worker dies in the middle of a /run, the client sees a dropped connection. With checkpointing on, it does not send the /run again; the controller sees no reply and retires the attempt everywhere, which frees the sessions it started. Sending it again would have run the attempt twice and left the first run's sessions with nothing to free them.

    When a restore repeats or goes unused

    If the same checkpoint is restored twice and the continued rollout made model calls in between, the second restore deletes what those runs left, fences included, and starts from exactly the saved lineage.

    • A restored rollout that is never sent again is deleted by the next commit that leaves it out, without a mark or a ledger fence, so the controller can still start that attempt later.
      • If deleting a ledger fails, the attempt stays unclaimed and a repeated commit deletes it again.
    • A new attempt that has already started is never deleted this way: its ledger is kept even if a commit leaves it out, so a running attempt's training rows are never lost.
      • This holds across policy servers that share one capture ledger: an attempt that any of them has started is marked on disk, and the others skip it.
    • A continued rollout sent through the flat-row wrapper with an explicit rollout ID such as r-a1 is decoded into rollout r, attempt 1, so it finds its restored episode.
    • Rollout collection refuses a dataset row whose own explicit ID ends in -a<N> when it loads.
    • A retry of a call that was continuing a restored cut continues the newest cut taken since, so it never receives a cut whose staged rows were deleted. With several workers it is generated again instead.

    When workers come and go

    How checkpoints handle workers that are lost, leave, or change in number:

    • If a worker of any server is lost between the commit's readiness check and its snapshot, the commit fails with 409 checkpoint_export_failed rather than writing a checkpoint without that worker's records.
      • The controller prepares again under a new checkpoint ID.
    • If a worker of a policy model server leaves, restore is refused until the server restarts, because its replacement cannot report what it served.
    • If the number of workers changes between a checkpoint and its restore, sessions are installed on the live workers.
      • The restore rewrites each one's routing claim to name its new worker, so old cookies keep reaching their sessions.

    Choices and the alternatives they rule out

    The mechanism as a whole is not small, because the problem spans several independent servers. Each part of it, though, is the simplest option we found that still meets the requirements. Where a cheaper option exists, the paragraphs below name it and explain which requirement it fails.

    Where state is saved

    Gym saves each rollout at the boundary after its last completed step rather than copying each server's memory. Copying the memory of several independent processes cannot produce one consistent moment unless every process stops at once, whereas boundaries are exactly where the protocol is already consistent.

    Servers declare what they can save in code rather than configuration, since only the author knows and a setting could claim support the code lacks. Every environment server, agent, resources server and the policy model server takes part by default, and anything it cannot save restarts. If servers had to opt in instead, one that did not would be missing from every checkpoint without any error. Taking part by default costs some repeated work, never correctness.

    What happens to work in progress

    The policy model holds undelivered responses instead of waiting for generations to finish, which keeps prepare to seconds rather than minutes. The agent is still at its boundary before the call, so making the call again after a crash is exact. Generation cuts stay optional for the same reason: requiring every generation to continue would make every checkpoint depend on every inference worker, while a missing cut only means the call is generated again.

    Gym also does not hold finished results until the controller confirms receipt. A result the controller never received is simply a rollout still in flight in the controller's checkpoint, so it restarts, which is always correct, and dropping the acknowledgement removes a whole protocol along with the ways it could stall. Rollouts that cannot be saved are reported rather than waited for, because waiting stopped every checkpoint behind one such rollout and discarded its progress even when nothing crashed.

    How state reaches its end of life

    Retire stops the work and frees the state before it replies. Freeing in the background, or expiring state after a time, would depend on requests never arriving late, which Gym cannot promise. The refusal that outlives a retire ends with an explicit forget for the same reason: only the controller knows when a rollout is finished for good, and a time limit would delete the entry while a late request could still arrive. More generally, Gym has no time-based cleanup anywhere, because a cutoff can delete state a long rollout still uses and leaves everything else in place until it passes.

    A /run is never sent twice with checkpointing on. Sending it again after a dropped connection runs the attempt twice and strands the first run's sessions, whereas not sending it costs only one rerun of that rollout as its next attempt.

    How the order and the files stay consistent

    Gym decides the checkpoint order because it depends on which Gym server calls which. Keeping the order inside Gym lets the controller treat Gym as one system and makes it impossible to get the order wrong from outside.

    Each checkpoint is written once, to files that never change once named. Rewriting the state on every repeated commit could change a checkpoint after part of it was published, while naming the records file after its content and creating the manifest only once means a published checkpoint cannot change and racing writers cannot mix their files.

    Requests find their worker through a routing claim per session ID, kept as one file in a directory the server's workers share.

    • The router reads the session ID the client already sends, in the session cookie, the MCP session token, or the body of a session start or close, so the client carries no worker identity.
    • A claim is removed when its session ends, so the directory holds only live sessions.
    • A restore moves a session by rewriting its claim, so a restore can change the number of workers.

    How long checkpoints take

    These runs used one workstation with every Gym server and a fake inference backend. Each rollout was a single_agent_turn weather episode with token capture and generation cuts on, and each rollout's second model call was held so that most rollouts were in flight at the checkpoint. Each run took a checkpoint, killed every Gym process, restarted Gym, restored, and ran the new attempts to completion.

    RolloutsPolicy workersIn flight and savedPrepare (s)Commit (s)Restore (s)New attempts that failed
    8,00014,2010.670.600.600
    8,00024,0830.560.690.560
    16,000214,3207.574.644.970
    16,0002, second run12,2283.601.833.230

    These numbers come from the branches this stack was cut from, and at 16,000 rollouts almost all of the prepare time is the policy model's.

    The slow paths that were fixed

    PathBeforeAfterChange
    Cleaning up 16,000 restored rollouts over 96,000 ledger filesabout 19 min0.23 sList the directory once and index it by rollout, instead of scanning it again for each rollout.
    Importing ledgers for 15,686 episodes3.2 s1.5 sSkip syncing each file to disk, since the checkpoint is the durable copy, and sync the directory once.
    Committing 1,000 sessions of 350 KB11.5 s3.6 sCheck opaque state once and write it unchanged, instead of validating and copying it deeply.
    Restoring the same sessions6.0 s3.4 sThe same change when reading.

    Work the design repeats on purpose

    The design accepts some repeated work in order to stay correct, and none of it grows over the run.

    • A rollout that cannot be saved starts over after a crash, though without a crash it costs nothing.
    • A held model call is generated again after a crash unless its prefix was cut.
    • The policy model does not know which rollouts are restarts, so it still holds their model calls during a checkpoint and may cut them for nothing.
    • With several workers, commit and restore carry every worker's records through the coordinator's socket, with a 1 GiB limit per message, so a server with very large sessions would eventually need one records file per worker.

    How it is tested

    Example tests check what each operation does on its own. Most bugs found in review only appeared when operations overlapped or failed part way, so two kinds of tests cover that instead:

    • Contract tests over many inputs, wherever two pieces of code must agree: every payload the record check accepts is restored unchanged or fails the commit by name; every capture key built from a run request decodes back to the same rollout and attempt; every control route refuses an invalid request with a typed client error; every kind of corrupt manifest is a typed error.
    • Random sequences of operations against one participant in one process, and against a coordinator with several workers over its real socket.
      • Each seed interleaves episode steps with prepare, commit, resume, retire, forget and restore at short or long deadlines, while:
        • writes are held or fail;
        • cleanup is slow;
        • a worker's close fails;
        • workers join;
        • checkpoints restore onto a different number of workers.
      • After every step:
        • admission is open everywhere when idle;
        • every worker refuses the same retired attempts as its coordinator;
        • every manifest verifies and stores the checkpoint's first export;
        • no manifest appears after resume;
        • no commit includes a retired attempt or a running restart;
        • every committed checkpoint restores.
      • Run against earlier versions of the stack, these fail on the bugs review found there.
    • Process-level tests start real Gym servers against a fake inference backend, checkpoint them mid-episode, kill them, restore, and check the exact model calls that follow, with one and with two workers per server. They include a deployment that mixes a saved environment with a restart-only one, and rollout collection preempted by a signal and resumed.
    • Every new test is checked against the code before its change, where it must fail.
    • An adversarial review pass before each push, reading the change for overlapping operations, partial failures, mismatched contracts, untyped errors and unbounded state.

    Known gaps

    Each gap below describes what Gym does today, what goes wrong, and the change that would fix it. Where Gym falls back to restarting a rollout or failing a checkpoint, the result is slower but still correct. The gaps tagged fixed could produce a wrong or failed rollout, or leave state behind, and are fixed in the stack; they stay here so reviewers can see what changed.

    A new model call during a checkpoint waits instead of failing fixed

    The policy model used to answer a new call during a checkpoint with 409 checkpoint_admission_closed.

    • Simple Agent coped by returning to its boundary, but a restart keeps running through the checkpoint, and an agent without hooks would have shown the error to the model or failed the rollout.
    • A new call now waits until resume before it is admitted, as a resources server's requests already did.
      • Because a waiting call is never admitted, prepare does not count it.
      • If its attempt is retired while it waits, it is refused at once with checkpoint_stale_attempt instead of running after resume.
      • It stays refused after the controller forgets the rollout, even if the retire was cut short.
      • The retire returns only after every waiting call of its attempts has left.
    • The proof refinement agent's retry loop for the old refusal is gone, since nothing sends that refusal any more.

    A rollout sent after the last checkpoint is never sent again as the same attempt fixed

    After a crash, the evaluation controller used to send every unfinished rollout outside the checkpoint again with the same attempt number, and nothing retired the earlier run's copy.

    • A harness from that run could still be alive in a remote sandbox, and its calls would have been accepted into the new run.
    • Rollout collection now keeps a dispatch log, described under evaluation runs.
      • On resume it retires the last attempt the previous run sent of every unfinished rollout it does not restore, then sends the next one.
      • Only rows that were actually sent are retired, so resuming a large evaluation retires only the rows its previous run sent and did not finish, not every row it has left.
    • The attempt number is excluded from every metric, so the bump changes capture keys but not results.

    Saving an opaque harness through sandbox snapshots needs two more pieces open

    An agent can already save a harness running in a microVM-backed sandbox through its session hooks, but two things are missing before that works end to end.

    • Nothing tells a server when a checkpoint is deleted, so the snapshots its saved state names would never be freed.
      • The controller needs to pass the IDs of the checkpoints it keeps so servers can free the rest.
    • The harness is usually waiting on a model or tool call at the moment its sandbox is paused.
      • After a crash, that call's connection points at a server that no longer exists and carries the old attempt.
      • The restored servers refuse that attempt with checkpoint_stale_attempt, because the restore marks the attempt it replaces.
      • The restored harness must have that call reach the restored model under the next attempt, either through the harness's own retry or through something in front of it that resends the call.

    A session start sent twice can leave a copy on another worker open

    If a session start's reply is lost while both servers keep running, the caller sends it again, and with several workers on the receiving server the second request can land on a different worker. The first copy then stays on its worker with nothing to free it until the server restarts. Not resending a session start once it may have been received, or routing session starts by session ID, would close this.

    A tool call on a closed or never-seeded session is not refused open

    A resources server checks a tool call's attempt only when it tracks the call's session.

    • A call with a valid MCP token after /close_session, or one that names a session the server never seeded, still runs its tool.
      • Any state it creates is outside every checkpoint and every retire.
    • The same call is a bug with checkpointing off, so the fix lands on main for both modes:
      • refuse a call on a session that is not open;
      • revoke a session's MCP token when it closes;
      • bind the default seed's cookie session to its resources session ID.
    • With checkpointing on, the resources participant's is_open answers whether a session is open.

    A crash right after a group's comparison delays its members slow

    Members that had not recorded their reward wait 30 minutes, fail and restart from their input. Recording the group's result before replying to any member would remove the wait.

    The evaluation controller repeats a retire that fails fixed

    Rollout collection used to log a failed batch of retires and move on, so the servers that missed it kept the attempts' state for the rest of the run. It now keeps every attempt whose retire failed and repeats them before the next checkpoint and again when the run ends. A forget that fails was already safe, because the run forgets every rollout it retired or restored and has not yet forgotten when it ends.

    A harness that outlived a crash is refused by the restored servers fixed

    Only a retire used to mark an attempt, so after a restore nothing refused the attempt that a continued rollout replaced.

    • A harness of that attempt that survived the crash, for example in a remote sandbox, could still call the restored servers and write into the continued rollout.
    • A restore now marks every episode in its scope on every participant and every worker, before any work its deadline limits.
      • Those servers refuse the old attempt with checkpoint_stale_attempt until the controller forgets the rollout.
    • The controller therefore forgets restored rollouts as well as retired ones.
      • Rollout collection does so once the replacement replies or when the run closes.

    A replayable verification keeps its session until the close fixed

    Coordination prepares environment servers before resources servers.

    • An environment server inside a replayable /verify keeps the boundary from before the verification.
    • If the verification finished before the resources server prepared, the resources server used to end the session, so the checkpoint held no session state for the verification a restore runs again.
    • A caller that closes the session after a replayable verification now says so with the x-ng-checkpoint-close-follows header.
      • The resources server keeps the session tracked and exported until that close, a declared end, or a retire.
      • single_agent_turn, the UserSim environment server, the sandboxed Hermes agent and Simple Agent's own /run send it.
    • A verification without the header, or one the checkpoint waits for, still ends the session at once, so a caller that never closes cannot leave it tracked.

    A request that names no attempt cannot change a restored session fixed

    An environment server's direct HTTP grant used to give the agent the bare resources server address and the session cookie.

    • A tool call with the cookie alone names no attempt, so after a restore the replaced attempt's harness could still change the restored state and claim the session.
    • With checkpointing on, the grant now carries the seeding attempt's rollout prefix.
      • Simple Agent sends each tool call under the prefix of the activation it serves, which after a restore is the replacement.
    • A request on a restored session that names no attempt, by rollout prefix or MCP token, is refused with checkpoint_rollout_id_required before it can change or claim the session.

    A restart another stage reported no longer holds up prepare fixed

    Each participant used to count as restarts only the episodes it found out about itself.

    • An environment server marks an episode a restart when its resources server is restart-only or it grants MCP access.
    • The agent serving that episode still treated it as one to save, so a slow tool call between two boundaries held up the agent stage of prepare for an episode the commit would leave out anyway.
    • Coordination now sends each later stage the restarts every earlier stage reported.
      • Each participant leaves those episodes out of its blockers and its export until the checkpoint resumes or aborts.
      • The resources server likewise stops waiting for requests in flight on their sessions.
      • With several workers, every worker is told.

    A run that skips verification parks at its return boundary fixed

    Simple Agent's legacy /run with verification skipped used to return its configured reward without recording a boundary. If a checkpoint finished preparing while the turn loop's reply was on its way back, the run finished during the checkpoint, and the commit held nothing to continue it from, so a restore ran the model and tool loop again. It now records the same return boundary as a verified run, waits there until resume, and a run restored at that boundary returns the recorded result.

    A commit never exports a checkpoint twice fixed

    A commit that failed because its export failed, or because the participant was no longer ready, could be repeated, and the repeat exported again. By then an episode could have moved to a later boundary than the other participants had committed, so the checkpoint would have mixed two cuts. Such a failure now ends the checkpoint: every commit for that ID is refused with 409 checkpoint_export_failed, and the controller resumes and prepares again under a new checkpoint ID. Storing records that were already exported is still repeated.

    A restored attempt sent as a flat row continues fixed

    The legacy flat-row wrapper built its episode ID from a row's rollout ID and its attempt index separately. An explicit rollout ID that already carried the attempt, such as r-a1 for a restored attempt, was rejected, because a rollout ID must not end in the reserved attempt suffix. The wrapper now decodes the row the way the agent does: r-a1 is attempt 1 of rollout r, a row without the suffix uses _ng_attempt_index, and a row that sets both fails. A restored turn sent through the wrapper now reaches the typed single_agent_turn request path as its next attempt and continues from its boundary.

    Policy servers that share a capture ledger never delete each other's restored rows fixed

    When several policy model servers capture into one ledger, for example a policy model and its reasoning-off variant, each one deletes the restored attempts that its commit's scope leaves out and that it has not served.

    • A server that a restored attempt never called could therefore delete the ledger the other server was continuing, and the attempt's training rows would be lost.
    • Checking for rows would not prevent this, because a call held for the checkpoint has written none yet.
    • The first admitted call of a restored attempt now creates <capture key>.lineage.started with O_CREAT|O_EXCL under the rollout's lock.
      • The deletion skips every attempt with that marker.
      • The marker ends with the attempt's ledger.
    • The deletion also removes the ledger before the server drops its record of the restored attempt, so a deletion that fails is tried again by the repeated commit instead of leaving the ledger behind.

    A worker lost just before the snapshot fails the commit fixed

    On a server with several workers, a commit checks readiness and then asks every worker for its records. A worker lost between those two steps takes its records with it, and without a check the commit would write a checkpoint that is missing that worker's sessions. The snapshot now fails unless every expected worker answers, so the commit fails with 409 checkpoint_export_failed and the controller prepares again under a new checkpoint ID.

    A replay step that fails during a checkpoint cannot end its episode early fixed

    When a replay step raises while a checkpoint is open, its episode is saved with no boundary and starts over after a crash. If the error reached the episode at once, its cleanup could close its sessions and its /run could reply while Gym is prepared, so the servers' state and the controller's list would change after the checkpoint counted them. The episode now waits at its cleared boundary until resume without holding up the checkpoint, and only then does the error reach its cleanup and its reply.

    A resources server never loses a session change to a client disconnect fixed

    A resources server learns that a session started or ended from the response to /seed_session, /close_session or /verify. If it recorded the change only after the reply was sent, a client that disconnected in between would cancel the request after the handler had already changed the session, and the server would lose track of a live session or keep tracking one that had ended. The change is now recorded when the response starts, before the reply is sent, while the request still counts as in flight.

    A session start in flight on a restart-only server is reported as a restart fixed

    A restart_only server never holds up a checkpoint, so prepare does not wait for its session starts. Without more, a start still in flight would be on no list: its episode would not yet be a restart, and the controller could continue a rollout whose resources server saved nothing. The server now lists the episode of every session start in flight as a restart, since that start's reply will say so, and the commit leaves it out.

    Files left by a killed process are removed by the next server fixed

    Every crash used to leave files behind:

    • A server with several workers put its coordinator socket at $TMPDIR/ng-<kind>-<pid>-<random>.sock and never removed it.
    • Session routing removed its directory of worker sockets only on a clean exit.

    Each server process now has one runtime directory, /tmp/ng-<pid>-<random>/, that holds its coordinator socket and its workers' private sockets and is removed when the process exits.

    • Creating one first removes those that killed servers left behind. A directory counts as left behind only if:
      • its owning process no longer exists, and
      • none of its sockets accepts a connection.
    • The second check protects a live server in another container that shares /tmp but not the process namespace.
    • Neither check is about age, so a live server's directory is never removed.
    • A connection that times out counts as alive, so a busy server is never mistaken for a dead one.

    A write killed in the middle can also leave .records.jsonl.<random> or .manifest.json.<random> inside a participant's part of a checkpoint. These need no change: nothing reads them, because the manifest names the real file, and they go when the controller deletes that checkpoint.

    A dataset rollout ID that names an attempt is refused when it loads fixed

    An explicit rollout ID that ends in -a<N> always means attempt N of the rollout before the suffix, which is how NeMo RL names a restored attempt.

    • Without a check:
      • a dataset row whose own ID ended that way would be read as an attempt of another rollout;
      • a resume retry that stamps the next attempt on the row would fail in the middle of the run, because the body would name an attempt twice.
    • Rollout collection refuses such a row with an error naming its line when its input or its materialized rows load.
    • A body that sets such an ID and also a nonzero _ng_attempt_index is refused.
    • A dataset whose own IDs end in -a<N> must rename them.

    A commit that reports success is durable fixed

    When a repeated commit finds its manifest already published, the write that published it may have failed before syncing the participant's directory, so a host crash could still lose the manifest's directory entry. A repeated commit that finds its manifest syncs the directory before it reports success.

    A retry continues the newest generation cut fixed

    A call restored with a cut keeps that cut until it delivers its response, so a retry can continue it again. If the call is still undelivered at the next checkpoint, that checkpoint keeps only the staged rows of the call's newest cut, so a retry that continued the restored cut could receive a cut whose staged rows were already deleted. After each cut round, the newest cut replaces the restored cut a live retry would use. With several workers, a worker never gives back a restored cut that a call used, so a retry of that call is generated again instead.

    A session start that finishes after its retire never becomes live fixed

    A retire waits for the session starts of its attempts, but a start can still finish after the attempt was retired, for example when the retire was cut short while it waited. Without more, its session would become live once the controller forgot the rollout, so it would be exported, restored and admitted. Such a session is a retired session instead: it is refused, never exported, and holds up checkpoints until a repeated retire frees it. Forget is refused with checkpoint_retire_incomplete while such a start is in flight or such a session is not yet freed.

    A session that a protocol route starts after a retire costs another retire round slow

    A retire waits for the session starts of its attempts that are in flight, on every route the server declares, a Gymnasium /reset included, so it frees the sessions they create. A start still waiting for a checkpoint to end is refused once its attempt is marked retired.

    A /run the controller itself sends twice open

    A second /run for an attempt that is already running can end the live episode. Making /run idempotent is planned as separate work.

    A restored cut can be lost with several workers compute only

    A worker takes a restored cut when it claims it, so if the claim times out the call is generated again, which costs compute but is still correct. A worker also never gives back a restored cut that a call used, so a retry of that call is generated again rather than continuing a cut whose staged rows a later checkpoint may have deleted.

    What any controller must do

    Gym's guarantees hold only if the controller does its part, and each rule below covers something Gym cannot enforce on its own.

    • Pause between prepare and resume. Stop sending rollouts and stop anything that consumes them, and do not read capture manifests or call the capture retire and delete routes while Gym is prepared or committed.
    • Leave restarts out of the commit. Build the commit list with PrepareResult.continued, and keep naming each continued rollout in every commit until its next attempt has been sent.
    • Wait for replies already on the way, but never for a restart. Before building the checkpoint's list of rollouts, wait for every outstanding /run whose rollout is neither in the commit nor a restart. A restart keeps running through the checkpoint, its next model call waits for resume, and after a crash it starts over from its input.
    • Publish before resuming. Publish the checkpoint only after every commit has succeeded, then call resume.
    • Record what you send, and retire it before sending again.
      • Record each attempt somewhere that outlives your process before you send it, including the rollouts sent after your last checkpoint.
      • After a crash:
        • retire the last recorded attempt of every rollout that will start over, then send it from its input as the next attempt;
        • send continued rollouts as their next attempt.
      • In a flat row, name the attempt either as an <id>-aN rollout ID or with _ng_attempt_index, not both.
      • Never give a dataset row an explicit ID that ends in -a<N>, because that suffix always names an attempt.
      • Restore a checkpoint only if no later run of yours sent its rollouts again.
    • Resume before retiring a straggler. To give up on a rollout that blocks prepare, resume first, retire it, then prepare again.
    • Forget when finished. Call forget once a retired rollout can never run again, and do the same for every restored rollout once it is finished for good, whether or not its replacement was sent. A restore leaves the same refusal for the attempt it replaces as a retire does. A forget refused with checkpoint_retire_incomplete means a resources server still holds a session of a retired attempt, so repeat the retire, then the forget.
    • Repeat a call that fails until it succeeds. No call is atomic across servers, so a retire or forget that fails partway must be repeated, or the servers that missed it keep the attempt's state or its entry. The exception is a commit refused with checkpoint_export_failed, for example because a worker was lost before the snapshot: that checkpoint is over, so resume and prepare again under a new checkpoint ID.
    • Delete checkpoint directories you do not keep. That includes directories from commits that were never published, which may hold partial records or temporary files from a crashed write.
    • Keep each group's group attempt. Changing it on restore would leave grouped verification waiting forever.

    Control API

    Every participating server exposes the same bearer-protected routes. Gym's checkpoint coordination calls them in the required order; the training framework calls the coordination.

    RouteValid in phaseEffect
    POST /ng-control/v1/checkpoint/prepareidle, preparingclose admission, then wait until ready or the deadline; report blockers, and the restarts that never block
    POST …/retireidle, restoredmark the named attempts' rollouts before any deadline-limited work, stop their work, including policy calls still waiting at closed admission, which stay refused even after forget, wait for it, free their state, then reply with retired_count; refused while a checkpoint is open
    POST …/forgetidle, restoredstop refusing these rollouts' retired or replaced attempts, once the controller is done with them for good; reply with forgotten_count; a resources server refuses it with 409 checkpoint_retire_incomplete, changing nothing, while a session start of a retired attempt is in flight or a retired session is not yet freed
    POST …/commitpreparedre-check readiness, export once, only live records inside the commit's scope, write records then manifest; a retry that finds the manifest already published syncs the participant's directory before it succeeds; a retry awaits the same write, or stores the same export again if storing failed; idempotent; a scope that names a restart is refused with 409 checkpoint_restart_in_scope; a failed export, such as one missing a worker lost before the snapshot, or readiness lost before the export started, ends the checkpoint, and every commit for that ID is refused with 409 checkpoint_export_failed
    POST …/restoreidle, fresh processmark the attempts in scope as retired before any deadline-limited work, read and validate the records in scope in one streaming pass, install them under the next attempt, stay closed; a retire waits for an install that outlived its deadline
    POST …/resumeany non-idlestop an unfinished write, so no manifest appears after it returns; reopen admission and let parked work continue; also the abort path; after a failed restore, retry a reopen that failed, under any checkpoint ID
    GET …/statusanyphase, checkpoint ID, readiness report, checkpoint mode, and retired_rollouts, the rollouts retired or restored and not yet forgotten; a resources server also reports whether its verification may be replayed
    POST /ng-control/v1/generation-cut (inference worker)—stage the prefix of each in-flight call and return a receipt

    Coordination order:

    • prepare environment servers → policy model → agents → resources.
    • Commit in any order.
      • Every commit is scoped to the episodes the controller continues: those in flight except the restarts, which PrepareResult.continued leaves out, and each unclaimed restored episode under its replacement attempt.
      • After a commit writes its files, each participant also deletes the restored episodes that are neither running nor in the commit's scope.
      • It does not retire them: the controller may still start those rollouts over as the same attempt, so nothing may refuse that attempt later, such as a capture-ledger fence.
      • A replacement attempt that has started is never deleted this way.
      • On policy servers that share a capture ledger, an attempt that any of them has started is skipped by all of them.
      • The ledger is deleted before the participant drops its record of the attempt, so a deletion that fails is tried again.
    • Resume resources → policy model → agents → environment servers.
    • Retire callers before callees: environment servers → agents → policy model and resources together, each replying only after the attempts' work has stopped.
    • Restore is all or nothing: if any participant fails, coordination retires the replacement attempts everywhere, which frees their restored state, and resumes every participant.
      • The training framework restarts those rollouts from their input as later attempts.
      • A restore gives each participant every episode it continues, including ones the participant holds no record of, so a participant that keeps files per episode clears what a dead execution left.
      • A restore that misses its deadline reopens admission only once its install has finished.
      • A resume that comes first waits for that install within its own deadline.

    Replies stay small for large calls. Retire replies with retired_count, the number of distinct attempts it was given, and forget with forgotten_count, the number of distinct rollouts, rather than every ID. Commit's episode_ids and restore's restored stay exact lists of the attempts exported and installed. Each server validates a control request once, and coordination encodes each request body once for every participant it reaches.

    Before its own barrier, the training framework waits for the replies to its outstanding /run calls whose episodes are neither in the commit nor reported as restarts. It never waits for a restart, which keeps running through the checkpoint and starts over from its input after a crash. Those episodes finished before prepare was ready, so their replies are already in flight. This replaces a completed-result acknowledgement protocol: Gym never holds a finished result waiting for an acknowledgement, and a lost reply can never block a checkpoint.

    NeMo RL as the controller

    In training, NeMo RL's Gym actor is the controller. It calls the coordination functions directly and never addresses an individual Gym server, so the participant order lives entirely in Gym. Its own sequencing code for Gym's servers can be deleted.

    Pausing training around a checkpoint

    Between prepare and resume, NeMo RL pauses rollout dispatch, the trainer actors and the trajectory assembler actors, because any of them consuming or retiring rollouts during that window could break the cut Gym is writing.

    • NeMo RL saves its own checkpoint after Gym's commit has succeeded, records which rollouts continue and which restart, and only then resumes Gym.
    • Rollouts whose replies were already on the wire must be collected before NeMo RL builds that list.
    • NeMo RL never waits for a restart:
      • a restart keeps running through the checkpoint;
      • its next model call waits for resume;
      • after a crash it starts over from its input.
    • A rollout whose replay step failed while Gym was prepared replies only after resume, so it stays in the list and starts over from its input after a crash.
    • If a commit fails with checkpoint_export_failed, for example because a worker of a Gym server was lost before the snapshot, NeMo RL resumes Gym and prepares again under a new checkpoint ID instead of repeating the commit.

    Token data across the checkpoint

    The policy model's commit reply lists the staged token-store keys the checkpoint still refers to, both as one list and per rollout.

    • NeMo RL keeps the rows of the rollouts it continues.
    • Rows belonging to calls the checkpoint left out become orphans that are masked from training.
    • With generation cuts on, NeMo RL's inference workers stage each cut prefix through the worker helpers in #3884, and the restored call continues it after the crash.
    • If that call is still undelivered at a later checkpoint, a retry continues the newest cut taken since, because the later checkpoint keeps only that cut's staged rows.

    NeMo RL also owns capture cleanup: it retires a rollout's capture once the result has been consumed or abandoned, and deletes it once nothing can still write to it. Those routes refuse with 409 during a checkpoint, so NeMo RL retries them after resume.

    If NeMo RL runs several policy model servers over one capture ledger, such as a policy model and its reasoning-off variant, a restored attempt's ledger stays as long as any of them has started the attempt. A capture ledger that NeMo RL supplies itself must implement mark_started() and delete_unstarted() as well as export, import, retire and delete, or the policy server fails at startup.

    After a crash

    After a restore, NeMo RL sends each continued rollout again as its next attempt and Gym continues it from its boundary.

    • A flat row may carry that attempt in its rollout ID, as <id>-aN, and the flat-row wrapper decodes it into rollout and attempt the way the agent does.
      • The suffix -a<N> is reserved for this, so a dataset must not give a rollout its own ID that ends in it.
      • A row must not set such an ID together with a nonzero _ng_attempt_index.
    • For each restart, and for every unfinished rollout that was not in the checkpoint, NeMo RL first retires the last attempt and then sends the next attempt from its input.
    • A continued rollout needs no retire, because the restore already refuses the attempt it replaces on every server.
    • Groups for GenRM keep their group attempt, so the group re-forms once every member has verified again.

    Ending refusals

    NeMo RL must call forget once a retired rollout is finished for good, and once a restored rollout is, because a restore refuses the attempt it replaces exactly as a retire does.

    • Otherwise every Gym server keeps one entry per retired or restored rollout for the rest of the run.
    • This requirement is new to NeMo RL's side and is tracked on NVIDIA-NeMo/RL#4549, which must cover restored rollouts as well as retired ones.
    • If a forget returns checkpoint_retire_incomplete, a resources server still holds a session of a retired attempt, for example one that a session start or a protocol route registered after the retire.
      • NeMo RL repeats the retire before it repeats the forget.

    Evaluation runs as the controller

    In evaluation runs, Gym's rollout collection is the controller, since it is the process that sends the rows. With checkpoint_dir set, it checkpoints on SIGUSR1 and keeps running, checkpoints on SIGTERM and stops, which lets a scheduler such as Slurm checkpoint just before a preemption, and can also checkpoint on a timer with checkpoint_every_s.

    Each checkpoint:

    1. stops starting new rows;
    2. prepares;
    3. commits the rows whose /run has not replied, except the restarts;
    4. writes the run's manifest with both lists;
    5. publishes it by pointing LATEST at it.
    • The checkpoint just published is always kept, plus the newest of the others, so a clock that steps back never deletes the checkpoint LATEST names.
    • A signal or timer that fires during startup waits until the run has reset or restored its state.
    • A restore holds the checkpoint lock, so a checkpoint never overwrites the progress being recovered.
    • Rollout collection is the only owner of SIGTERM for the run; other reports that want it, such as the timing table, print from its handler before the checkpoint.
    • A checkpoint the timer started is finished before the run closes, and a cancelled checkpoint still resumes every participant.
    • A row that passed the dispatch gate can still reach the environment server after prepare closed admission.
      • The server refuses it with checkpoint_admission_closed before anything of the episode runs.
